en: The meaning is that [the property] exists even in the thread which is the locus of the final conjunction and is distinct from the threads of the cloth consisting of a thousand threads. He states what is intended by the author of the *Dīdhiti*: "Let it be so even thus. Regarding the state of having a counter-correlate (*sapratiyogikatva*), the point is that since there is no evidence for its being an absence (*abhāvatva*), the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) is not established. How?

The intention of the objector is that [the cognition] "red does not exist" has absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) as its object, because cognitions such as "it does not exist" have absolute non-existence as their content.
However, it should be understood that the intention of the proponent (siddhāntin) is that there is no evidence for such being the case.
Regarding the doubt stated by the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*): [it concerns] the time of the jar...

The meaning is: [this is said] in response to the objection that, even if the relation with the absence of a jar were not a constituent factor, there would still be the undesirable consequence of a cognition of the absolute absence of a jar at the time of the prior absence (*prāgabhāva*) of a jar. Regarding the phrase "the cognition in the form 'red color does not exist'": [an opponent might ask], "But surely such a cognition does not have absolute absence as its object."

In response to the objection that it has already been stated that only prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) can be such [objects], he says: "of that" (*tasya*). This means "of the cognition 'it does not exist'.

The meaning is: because it apprehends a general absence (*sāmānyābhāva*), that is, because its object is an absence whose counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) is delimited by a general property (*sāmānyadharma*).
The ellipsis is to be supplied as follows: "because it is not accepted that destruction and prior non-existence possess a counter-correlativity delimited by a general property (*sāmānyadharma*).
Now, [one might object] regarding the cognition "it does not exist":

Anticipating the objection that there is no evidence for the view that [the cognition] has as its object merely an absence whose counter-positive is delimited by a general property (*sāmānyadharma*), he refutes it with the words "And not... (*na ca*). Regarding the phrase "pūrvāpara...": it refers to a jar that was first red, then black, then red, then black, and then red again.

The meaning is: "in that state of intermediate redness. However, this undesirable consequence does not arise in a case where there are three successive stages of redness, because it is possible not to accept that the destruction of such redness and the absence of its adventitious quality (parāgabhāva) serve as the restrictors of the cognition in the form "it does not exist.
[End of] Rāmarudrī. But in the aforementioned case...

It should be noted that even in the state of being dark-colored (*śyāmatā*), it is necessary for those two [the pot and its blackness] to be restricted by such a cognition, because of the occurrence of such a cognition. "By way of non-pervasive occurrence" (*avyāpyavṛttitvena*) means "by way of temporal non-pervasive occurrence."
"Upon the destruction of another entity" means:

upon the destruction of air-contact and so forth that is co-located with [the color] and arises at the same time as the destruction and arising of the red color. "Due to complexity" means: because there is no decisive evidence [to prefer one over the other], [one would have to postulate] an infinite number of destructions and so forth.
The meaning is that it would result in the conceptualization of a counter-positiveness delimited by redness (*raktatvāvacchinnapratiyogitākatva*), which is cumbersome (*gaurava*).

The nature of absence as being identical with its locus (*adhikaraṇarūpatā*) was raised as a doubt in the root-text; regarding that, he states the connection with the preceding section: "Now, [as for] absence... and so on. [This refers to] the word "distinct" (*atirikta*).

It is not possible for [the word] to have a meaning distinct from the categories already established, because even non-existence (*abhāva*) has been established by the Naiyāyikas as one of them; therefore, he says "distinct from existence" (*bhāvātiriktā*) to exclude that.
As for the claim that "non-existence is of the nature of its locus": even though the absence of fragrance may take the form of water and so forth...

It should be understood that the intention of the Prābhākaras is as follows: water and the like are not perceptible by the olfactory organ simply by virtue of being water and so forth, because they lack odor; however, it is indeed accepted that those [entities] possess such perceptibility [by the olfactory organ] precisely insofar as they are odors. || 12 ||

Since the purpose of defining similarity and dissimilarity at the root [of the inquiry] has not been stated, he says "paraspara... (mutually... in order to demonstrate it. Regarding the phrase "jñānaviṣayatātvena" (by way of being the object of cognition):
being the non-counterpositive of an absence that possesses a locus is not what constitutes being purely positive (kevalānvayi), because even that which is purely positive...
Because non-existence exists as duality and so forth, [the definition] is not [too narrow];
rather, it is simply the state of possessing a property that is not a delimitor of the counter-correlativity (pratiyogitā) of a non-existence that has a locus.
And thus, even for a particular instance of objectivity residing in a jar or the like, by taking its nature as the objectivity of cognition (jñāna-viṣayatātva), [the definition applies]. (Rāmarudrī)

The point is that its status as a purely positive (kevalānvayi) property remains unimpaired. Regarding the phrase "connection with time": this is stated while accepting that even [entities] such as space (gagana) reside in time; for if non-occurrent entities like space did not reside in time, it would be impossible for existence (astitva) to be a purely positive property. This is correct.
This is so; otherwise, how could it be maintained that space and the like possess causality with respect to sound and other phenomena, as defined by their being invariably antecedent? || 13 ||

Desiring to avoid the deficiency [of his definition] regarding the six categories (*ṣaḍbhāvapadārtha*) by stating their common property (*sādharmya*) at the outset, he says: "Of substance and the rest" (*dravyādīnām*). Now, one might object:
in the verse, it was stated that the common property of the five categories beginning with substance is merely their multiplicity; how then, given that multiplicity, [is this not redundant]?

He dispels the doubt that "being a positive entity" (*bhāvatva*) was not mentioned as a point of similarity (*sādharmya*) in the *Muktāvalī* because it was not found in the original root text, by saying "and thus" (*evaṃ ca*). He states the agreement of the authors of the *Bhāṣya* regarding the aforementioned point, saying "for this very reason" (*ata eva*). Regarding the phrase "of the five positive entities" (*pañcabhāvānām iti*), he implies that if the authors of the *Bhāṣya* indeed accepted the inclusion of "being a positive entity" within the scope of the defining characteristic of the subject (*uddeśyatāvacchedaka*), [then it must have been intended].
The intended meaning is that one should say "the manifoldness of the five entities" instead of "of the five," thereby discarding the number five.

Now, regarding the phrase "residing in multiple entities": if "manifoldness" here refers to the numerical category of plurality (*bahutva-saṃkhyā*), then there would be the fault of under-extension (*avyāpti*) with respect to qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth, which lack such a number. And if it refers to being different from any single entity whatsoever, then...

There is over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to *samavāya* (inherence). If it is defined as the exclusion of a generality delimited by unity (*ekatvāvaccchinnasāmānyabheda*), and if that unity therein is of the nature of number (*saṃkhyārūpa*), then the aforementioned over-extension remains as it was. If, however, it is the state of being the object of a cognition whose sole content is that [unity], then there is non-establishment (*aprasiddhi*).

The inclusion of the term "existence" (*satyanta*) is for the purpose of defining "subsistence in multiple entities" (*anekabhāvavṛttitva*), in order to dispel the following doubt: since oneness in the form of being the object of a cognition whose content is its own measure (i.e., its own substrate) is a purely positive concomitant (*kevalānvayin*), there is no established instance of the difference from such a universal delimited by that [oneness]. Thus, the inclusion [of the term "existence"] serves to provide that definition.

It should be understood that the inclusion of both relations is also for the purpose of excluding that [over-extension]. Regarding the possession of an adjunct (*upādhimat*), he states the result of considering the relation in the *Rāmarudrī*: "By this," and thus it was not mentioned [separately].

When the possession of an adjunct is stated by way of its own nature (*svarūpeṇa*), in the case of substance-ness (*dravyatva*) and so forth, with respect to the spatial relation of essential nature (*daiśika-svarūpa-sambandha*)—

It should also be observed that there is no lack of pervasion (avyāpti) regarding substance and the other categories due to the absence of "pride" (māna). Avoiding the charge that the root text is deficient for failing to state the common properties (sādharmya) of the four categories, he says: "And also...
In the statement "the three beginning with existence possess existence," the common property of possessing existence is predicated with reference to the first triad.

That [converse] is prescribed, but that is improper because the word expressing the subject (uddeśya) must be mentioned first; for this very reason, the proposition (*pratijñā*) is "The mountain possesses fire" (*parvato vahnimān*) and not "The fire possesses the mountain" (*vahnimān parvataḥ*); thus, by way of application (*yojanayā*), [the author] dispels such a doubt.

He states that [the text] reveals the meaning obtainable from the *Muktāvalī* with the words "denoting the subject" (*uddeśyavācaka*). The point is that otherwise, because such a sentence would have an excessively clear meaning, the sentence beginning with "substance, quality, etc. (*dravyaguṇa-*) would be rendered entirely purposeless. Regarding this, [the definition of a category is] the state of possessing a limiting property (*upādhi*) that serves as a differentiator among the categories eternally inherent [in them].

The similarity between substance (*dravya*) and quality (*guṇa*) should be understood [as follows]. However, the similarity of substance alone will be stated by the author himself. Now, if "the state of being devoid of qualities" and so forth means "the state of possessing the mutual absence of qualities and actions," then there would be over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to substance, since that too possesses it.

To the objection that there is a difference between these two [states], he says: "And for that purpose... [He means] "there would be no visibility. The point is that color (*rūpa*) is the cause of visibility (*cākṣuṣatva*), and at the moment of production, that [color] is absent in the jar and so forth.
Now, even if one accepts the presence of color in the jar and so forth during the first moment, in the preceding moment...

Since the visual contact with the locus of the jar—which serves as the cause [of its perception]—is absent due to the absence of the jar itself, the visual perception of the jar and so forth is simply not possible in the first moment; how then can this undesirable consequence arise?
For even the inherence in that which is visually contacted (*cakṣuḥ-saṃyukta-samavāya*) is impossible at that time in the case of the jar and such objects during the moment of their production.

Since things such as pots do not exist [in that context], in reality, because it is necessary to include the qualification "fitness" (yogyatva) for the conjoined eye in order to exclude the perception of substanceness (*dravyatva*) and so forth in an atom (*paramāṇu*), there would otherwise result the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) with respect to the visual perception of a triad (*tryaṇuka*); therefore, [the definition] must be restricted to the state of being visually perceived as inherent in a substance other than a substance.

He provides the resolution with the intention that, since [the property] must be accepted as the delimitor of the effectness of inherence in what is conjoined (*saṃyuktasamavāya*), the perception of a jar or the like through "inherence in what is conjoined with the eye" is simply not possible— hence the phrase "because it is an accepted consequence" (*iṣṭāpatter iti*). And thus:

The point is that the visual perception of a jar and so forth occurs at the very third moment. Regarding the phrase "by way of either connection": this is merely prima facie; for, by parsimony (*lāghava*), [the definitions] should rather be "not residing in a quality-possessor" (*guṇavadavṛttitva*) and "possessing a property that does not reside in a quality-possessor" (*guṇavadavṛtidharmavattva*).
— Rāmarudrī.

Because it is more appropriate to speak [of this] precisely through the relation of being the very nature of the indicator (*daiśikasvarūpasaṃbandha*); for it is possible to establish the common property (*sādharmya*) by taking, for instance, the state of being the qualificandum of a true cognition whose mode is "quality-ness" (*guṇatva*) with respect to qualities and so forth. However...

In the definition of the second similarity—namely, "the state of possessing a delimitor that divides the categories [of existence], such as action" (karmavat)—it must be understood that, according to the method already stated, the inclusion of one of the two relations is necessary; for otherwise, since a category-delimiting delimitor such as "quality-ness" (guṇatva) does not exist in qualities and so forth by way of the relation of identity (svarūpa-sambandha), the definition would fail to apply. || 14 ||

[This is] because there is an absence of a factor that determines the locus-hood (*adhikaraṇatā-niyāmakatva*). Even if this were the case, as stated in the *Rāmarudrī*, then even the state of being an existent (*bhāvatva*) would not belong to universals (*sāmānya*) and so forth; for in those cases, the locus-hood of existence must be established precisely by taking the locus-hood of "being" (*sat*) with respect to the relation of co-location (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).

Nevertheless, the point is that the nature of being an entity (*bhāvatva*) consists solely in either inherence in existence (*sattā-samavāya*) or co-occurrence in the same substratum (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).

In reality, however, it should be noted that there is no fault whatsoever if the general absence (*sāmānyābhāva*)—whose counter-correlativity is delimited by the relation of inherence—is taken as the common property (*sādharmya*). And as for the claim that this is not possible:
The word "ca" (and) does not signify conjunction; for since the dimension of an atom is eternal,
it cannot be a cause by way of being time, nor can it be a cause by way of being an object in perception due to its being beyond the senses,
and thus its causality toward any other effect is impossible.
Because a conjunction [of causes] is impossible here, he states that the word *tu* has the sense of *tu* (the particle of distinction)—namely, "in the sense of *tu*. Now, one might object:

since the dimension of a triad (*tryaṇuka*) is of the same genus as atomic dimension (*aṇu-parimāṇa*) by virtue of being a dimension, and is superior to atomic dimension, the dimension of a dyad (*dvyaṇuka*) would also be a cause [for it]. To this, [he replies: no.
Anticipating the objection that "the stated rule would be violated," he says: "In this case, there is a commonality of genus.
The limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) that differentiate dimension (*parimāṇa*) are "atomicity" (*aṇutvatva*), "largeness" (*mahatvatva*), and so forth.
The phrase "because it would follow that it is not visible to the eye" implies the remainder: "because of the absence of largeness" (*mahatvābhāvāt*). This refers to the following.
The meaning is that [number] and so forth are the causes for dyads (*dvyaṇuka*) and other atoms (*paramāṇu*). "Later on" means in the section defining the qualities (*guṇanirūpaṇa*).
"Here" means in the context of largeness (*mahattva*) and generality (*sāmānya*). [Rāmarudrī: But [one might object] that in the case of yogic perception, the object...

To address the question of what logic applies in the absence of the object being a cause, he says: "Just as... Thus, even in the case of a yogic perception, if the object were its cause, there would be no direct perception of past or future objects; therefore, it must be admitted that the causality of the object pertains only to ordinary (laukika) perception.
The point is that the dharma produced by yoga (*yogajadharma*) is indeed an extraordinary sense-contact (*alaukikasannikarṣa*). Regarding "in one's own perception":
the point is that in the perception of the largeness residing in the self, the self itself is a cause by way of being the object (*viṣaya*).
Regarding "due to unfitness": otherwise, [if it were not so], the self would be atomic (*aṇu*) or would have the nature of a sense-organ and so forth.

The meaning is that there is no possibility of dispute. "An effect consisting of an entity other than that" means an effect consisting of an entity other than cognition (*jñāna*) and so forth. Although in the text of the Teacher [Vācaspati Miśra], it is stated with respect to effects other than the attributes of the knower (*jñātṛdharma*), [the term] "entity-ness" (*bhāvatva*)... [is used]. (Rāmarudrī)

Even so, since the dimension of a dyad (*dvyaṇuka*) is the cause of its own destruction, the term "sphericity" (*pārimāṇḍalya*)—if taken to mean the general category of atomic dimension (*aṇu-parimāṇa-sāmānya*)—would over-extend (*ativyāpti*) to the dimension of the dyad. Therefore, "being an entity" (*bhāvatva*) is included [in the definition]; that is, *bhāvatva*.
However, even in its own system (svamata), this must indeed be granted; otherwise, there would be over-extension (ativyāpti) in that very case.
The phrase "of color and so forth, which has not yet been produced" is a qualification [intended] for the color of an atom destroyed by heating (pākanaṣṭa-paramāṇu-rūpa) and the like;
therefore, prior to the destruction of even the color of an atom destroyed by heating—
There is no deficiency even if [the atom] acts as a producer of the color and other qualities of a dyad (*dvyaṇuka*), for what is intended here is the state of being a producer of an effect.

This is because dimension (*parimāṇa*) is generally a cause with respect to [another] dimension through the relation of inherence (*samavāya*), while sphericality (*pārimāṇḍalya*) is also a cause with respect to dimension through the relation of "inhering in that which inheres in itself" (*svāśrayasamavetatva*). Thus, sphericality is a cause.

The intention is to express the state of being a producer of an effect by virtue of possessing a causality that consists in intrinsic capability (*svarūpayogyatā*). And this [intrinsic capability] is not merely the possession of intrinsic capability while being qualified by the effect through the relation of immediate antecedence, because such a definition would apply even to spherical dimension (*pārimāṇḍalya*). Rather, it is as follows:

It is precisely the state of being the producer (*prayojaka*) of the effect's arising. Furthermore, this state of being a producer is of the nature of an essential relation (*svarūpa-sambandha*), as evidenced by the cognition "the production of the jar [is caused] by the staff"; this is how it should be understood. Although in our own system pleasure and pain are causes with respect to one's own perception, nevertheless, because the form of an atom is beyond the senses (*atīndriya*), [it cannot be perceived].

Since a non-existent entity (abhāva) is not a cause with respect to an existent effect (bhāvakārya), the lack of pervasion (avyāpti) remains exactly as it was. Nor can it be argued that because time, as a limiting adjunct (upādhi) for everything produced, possesses the nature of time, its causality toward an existent effect remains unimpaired; for if that were the case, it would follow that even the dimension (parimāṇa) of a dyad (dvyaṇuka) [would be a cause].

By way of defining time as the causal factor for entities, [the author] avoids the contradiction with the root text which states, "The atom, however, is not the cause of anything," by interpreting the term "causality" (*kāraṇatva*) as referring to causality characterized by a result that is not delimited by resulthood (*kāryatvānavacchinna-kāryatā-nirūpita-kāraṇatva*); thus, action itself is time.
Thus, because the recourse to the aforementioned view is necessary, the charge of over-narrowness (*avyāpti*) is unavoidable; therefore, this [position] is inconsistent.

Nevertheless, even in our own system, because the word "and" (*ca*) implies that specific qualities (*viśeṣas*) are also necessary, the charge of over-narrowness remains unavoidable; thus, this [position] is inconsistent. Even so, in our own system...

The sense is that by the word "ca" (and) in the phrase "viśeṣāśca," such a form is also included. Regarding the expression "in the case of being a staff" (daṇḍatvādau): this means [the state of] being invariably antecedent with respect to the location that is the locus of the jar. [This is] by way of the relation of "being the locus of its own locus. (Rāmarudrī) 2. By the relation of being the locus of its own locus.
The point is that even a stick, a potter, and so forth, are connected to the locus of the jar.

Regarding the phrase "delimited by jar-ness" (*ghaṭatvāvacchinna*): although it will be argued later that when the production of an effect is possible through those very factors delimited by the delimiters of their being invariably and antecedently present in a light manner, anything co-present with them is *anyathāsiddha* (redundantly established).

The author of the work will explain the definition of the fifth type of extraneous determination (*anyathāsiddhi*); thus, although that donkey’s status as a non-delimiter of its own necessary antecedence even with respect to the potness-qualified [pot] entails that the donkey is extraneously determined with respect to the potness-qualified [pot] as well, nevertheless—

Because simplicity (*lāghava*) exists in various forms— such as that produced by the body, that produced by a relation, and so forth— it is impossible to state a single, common definition for its being "otherwise established" (*anyathāsiddhatva*). This is because its opposite, complexity (*gaurava*), which consists in being constituted by this or that particular category (*padārtha*), is likewise distinct according to the difference between those respective individual instances.
Since the term "anyat" (other) implies a heavy conceptual burden, it ultimately results in the redundancy of the definition;

therefore, "being otherwise established" (*anyathāsiddhatva*) must be defined simply as "being distinct from those [factors]. Furthermore, in that case, since those things distinct from the necessary antecedents can be excluded by the very condition of being a "necessary antecedent," [the inclusion of the term "other" is superfluous].

Since it would involve excessive complexity (*gaurava*) for such infinite varieties of entities to enter into the definition of being "not otherwise established" (*anyathāsiddhi-śūnyatva*), those [entities] which, while being invariably antecedent to that effect,
are not considered to be its cause by virtue of being its causal factor— [are what are excluded].

The state of being "not otherwise established" (*anyathāsiddhi-śūnyatva*) is precisely its difference from that [the effect]. Thus, since the property of being that particular donkey lacks the status of being a delimitor (*avacchedaka*) of the invariable antecedence delimited by "pot-ness" (*ghaṭatva*), the meaning is that this donkey is not "otherwise established" with respect to the [effect] delimited by pot-ness. Nor is it the case that...

It should not be argued that the collection of absences delimited by "stick-ness" (*daṇḍatva*) and so forth, being a single unified [property], may be considered an extraneous cause (*anyathāsiddha*).

For if that were the case, since the absence of that [collection] could be established as the instrumentality (*karaṇatā*) of "stick-ness" itself, the remaining [members of the collection] would be redundant. Furthermore, it would follow that "stick-ness" and the like, which subsist in fewer instances, could not be the delimitors of instrumentality (*kāraṇatāvacchedaka*).

It should be understood that the absence of a collection of those [specific] differences is not something additional. Regarding the definition of causality as "belonging to a class of things that invariably precede" in order to establish causality in cases such as a staff standing in a forest, it follows that by virtue of the property of *dravyatva* (substantiality) and so forth, even jars, cloths, and the like would incur the status of being causes of a jar. Therefore—

He says: "and being of that same class. [Regarding] "stick-ness" (*daṇḍatva*) and so forth: one should not argue that the defect remains as it was because substance-ness (*dravyatva*) and the like—which possess stick-ness—are also indeed delimiters of invariable antecedence (*niyatapūrvavartitāvacchedaka*). [This is because] by the term "delimiter of invariable antecedence," [only those properties that are themselves causes are intended]. *Rāmarudrī*: By the phrase "delimiter of invariable antecedence," [the author intends to exclude non-causal properties].

This is because the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) for the necessary antecedence (*niyatapūrvavartitā*) has already been stated. Since "substance-ness" (*dravyatva*) is the delimiting factor for the necessary antecedence of a jar, if that alone were considered the nature of the jar's causality, it would entail the conceptualization of jar-causality in all infinite substances, resulting in complexity (*gaurava*). Therefore, the essence of the notion is that "stick-ness" (*daṇḍatva*) and so forth are themselves the simpler [delimiting factors]. And thus:

It is concluded that the definition of the cause of a jar (*ghaṭakāraṇatva*) is: being a property that delimits the state of being invariably antecedent to a jar, while existing as non-different from stickness, potter-ness, and substanceness. || 16 || 17 || When it is stated that "that which, by way of the relation of inherence (*samavāya*), produces an effect is the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) of that [effect],"...
Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that the potsherd and other such parts would be the inherent cause of the pot even by virtue of being "substance-ness" (*dravyatva*) and so on;
furthermore, there would be the consequence that what is delimited by "potsherd-ness" would likewise be such [an inherent cause] with respect to that which is delimited by "that-pot-ness" and so on.
Therefore, he explains: "delimited by which... [and] "for want of evidence."
The sense is that, in all cases, the destruction of a substance is possible solely through the destruction of its non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*).

Regarding the term "dyad" (*dvyaṇuka*): here, the word "dyad" refers to such things as a jar, which [is destroyed] merely through the destruction of its conjunctions, even without the destruction of the potsherds that constitute its origin.
The term "destruction" (nāśa) is also indicative of such things as the jar itself; therefore, there is no risk of [the definition] being too narrow.

Regarding the phrase "for two moments": even though the destruction of the inherent cause (samavāyikāraṇa) is the cause of the destruction of the substance, it is necessary that the jar and so forth persist for at least one moment after the destruction of the shards, existing without those shards for a time.

The phrase "dvayapada" refers to the following: [from] Rāmarudrī: [the objection] "because of the undesired consequence" (iṣṭāpatteḥ). Now, one might ask: when a substance is destroyed, the destruction of its inherent cause (samavāyikāraṇa) is also [a factor]; why is it mentioned separately?

Since the [phenomenon] is established by the mere postulation of causality, it is not appropriate to accept the persistence of a substance for two moments in the absence of an inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*). Nor should it be argued that there is mutual deviation (*vyabhicāra*) because substances produced from one another are destroyed by one another; for [the relation of cause and effect is defined by] immediate succession (*avyavahitottaratva*).
Since it is possible to exclude that [undesired consequence] by including [the property] within the scope of the delimiting condition (*kāryatāvacchedaka*) of the effect, he says:

"by another cause," etc. Now, [one might object]: with respect to a destruction whose counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) is a substance, by way of the relation of spatial qualification (*daiśika-viśeṣaṇatā*), [spatial qualification acts as the cause].
If causality were defined by the property of being the destruction of that which has as its counter-positive a non-inherent cause of a substance,
then in a case where the destruction of a cloth consisting of a thousand threads occurs due to the destruction of the conjunction of some particular thread,
the destruction of the cloth would arise even in those threads that are not the locus of the destruction of the thread-conjunctions [that caused it].

He raises an objection with the words "Now, [if... (*atheti*), intending that there would be the consequence of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) because destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) and prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) reside only in the locus of the counter-positive's inherence (*pratiyogisamavāyideśa*).
With the words "as the cause" (*hetutveti*), he indicates that there is also parsimony (*lāghava*) regarding the delimiting factor of causality (*kāraṇatāvacchedaka*). This is the sense.

"The consequence of momentariness" means that, starting from the very moment of its production, some form of destruction exists in things such as a jar; this is the intended sense. Now, in order to exclude momentariness, why not simply replace the condition "inherence in the same substratum as its own counter-positive" with "being produced by its own counter-positive"?
In response to the doubt, "Why is [the counter-positive] not established? he says: "its own counter-positive.

Since it is only pure inherence (*kevalasamavāya*) that serves as the delimitor of causality (*kāraṇatāvacchedaka*),

To dispel the doubt that the form of the skull and so forth does not exist in the locus of the form of the jar and so forth, he states the meaning of that [term]: "kāryaikārtha" (having the same object as the effect). This has been demonstrated; however, the point is that by that form, the inherence (samavāya) does not obtain the status of being the delimiting relation of causality (*kāraṇatāvacchedaka-sambandhatva*). Since it has been demonstrated that destruction must be stated as the cause for the destruction of a substance by way of its being the counter-positive (pratiyogitā) through the three aforementioned relations, and by way of its being destruction itself, the properties of effectness and causality are not delimited by the relation of "determining attribute" (daṇḍika-viśeṣaṇatā).
