He introduces the opinion of some [authorities] with the words "śabdāśrayatve" (as the substratum of sound) and "aṣṭadravye" (in eight substances).

The eight substances consist of the four beginning with earth (pṛthivyādi-catuṣṭaya) and the four beginning with time (kālādi-catuṣṭaya). Regarding the phrase "having apprehended the antecedence toward another," etc., it means having grasped the state of being a prior condition (pūrvavartitva) with respect to something else.
Immediately after "is apprehended," one must supply the phrase "it is otherwise established with respect to that.
In the expression "not establishing prior existence" (*pūrvavṛttitvānupapādaka*), "prior existence" should be qualified by its own locus (*svaniṣṭhatvena*);
otherwise, [the definition would fail] because the ether (*gagana*) is a cause of sound with respect to the activity of the throat and other organs that produce sound.

Otherwise, there would be no "establishment through another" (*anyathāsiddhatva*) [in the case of the agent], because that [status] consists in being a constituent of the word's being antecedent to the action residing in the agent. This is stated with reference to its residing in itself (*svaniṣṭhatva*).

It should be noted that even though the operation [of effort] residing in the vocal organs establishes the status of being a prior-occurring cause for the sound residing in the ear, it does not establish the status of being a prior-occurring cause for the sound residing in space; therefore, in relation to that [sound in space] as well, the sky (*gagana*) is "otherwise-established" (*anyathāsiddha*). Regarding the phrase "of many phonemes": now, an objection is raised:

Even if the specific property (*viśeṣa*) were the delimiting factor of causality (*kāraṇatāvacchedaka*), the lack of a decisive reason (*vinigamanāviraha*)—due to the fact that one could take each individual [letter] as the cause—is indeed unavoidable; therefore, out of dissatisfaction with this, he says: "of the letters" (*varṇānām*).
This is because it is precisely the existence of a cause qualified by the delimiting factor of causality that serves as the instigator of the production of the effect.
The point is that if the letter *ka* were non-existent in the sky, then other sounds would likewise not arise there.

However, it should be understood that this objection does not apply if the existence of the cause as characterized by its causal determinant (*kāraṇatāvacchedaka*) is what necessitates the production of the effect. Even though...

Although the ether (*gagana*) is a cause with respect to that which is delimited by "sound-ness" (*śabdatva*) by virtue of being the cause of sound, it does not constitute the fallacy of "being established otherwise" (*anyathāsiddhi*), because sound is not distinct from sound. Nevertheless, if the self were its own delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*), there would arise the fallacy of self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*) regarding the cognition of the delimiting factor of causality.

The pursuit of [properties] such as *itikartavyatātva* (the state of being a procedure) as the delimitors of causality is due to their being the causes for the apprehension of causality. Now, regarding the property of being space (*gaganatva*),
with respect to the delimitation of the immediately preceding moment—

It is not even possible for the ether (*gagana*) to possess the status of a "delimiting factor of necessary antecedence" (defined as being a non-delimiter of the counter-correlativity of an absence residing in the locus of a jar), because, since the ether does not reside [in space], there exists an absence of it in the locus of a jar by way of conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and other relations. Thus, regarding the ether...

If it is argued that the demonstration of "otherwise-establishment" (*anyathāsiddhi*) is useless for the purpose of excluding [the sky] from being a cause, we say no. This is because, even if [the sky] does not exist [as a substance], according to the view that existence (*vṛttitva*) is established through the relation of time (*kālikasaṃbandha*), it is possible for the sky to possess "invariably antecedent existence" (*niyatapūrvavṛttitva*) precisely through the relation of time; this should be kept in mind. Regarding the phrase "necessarily postulated" (*avaśyaklṛpta*): although...

Since smell and color arise at the same time, the prior non-existence (prāgabhāva) of smell and the prior non-existence of color are equally established as necessary; nevertheless, because the cognition of the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) is a cause for the cognition of a non-existence,
it is only the prior non-existence of smell that [is cognized] immediately after the presentation of the effect, namely smell and color.

A swift presentation [of the cause] is possible, but not for the prior absence of color (*rūpa-prāgabhāva*), because its presentation depends upon the cognition of color. Thus, by virtue of this ease of presentation, it is necessarily established that the prior absence of odor (*gandha-prāgabhāva*) alone is the invariably antecedent condition with respect to odor. This is so because [the absence of color] follows after the presentation of the effects produced by heating, namely odor and color.
However, the simultaneous presence of both odor and the prior absence of color is possible,
because the conjunction produced by the agent that effects the transformation of color is itself the meaning of the term "cooking" (pāka),
and thus the presence of color is also necessary; and so, in the case of what is not produced by cooking, with respect to odor—

The established meaning is this: since the production of the smell produced by baking (*pākaja-gandha*) is possible through the antecedent absence of smell (*gandha-prāgabhāva*) alone—which is necessarily established as an invariable antecedent—the antecedent absence of color (*rūpa-prāgabhāva*) with respect to that [smell] is "otherwise-established" (*anyathāsiddha*). Regarding the phrase "belonging to the class of pot" (*ghaṭajātīya*): it means belonging to the same class as that pot by virtue of being a pot (*ghaṭatva*).
The meaning of "dependent" (*pratītya*) is: in the case of the possibility of the production of that jar; the meaning is, in the case of the possibility of the production of that specific jar.

As for the phrase beginning with "But surely" (*nanu*): because odor and color are produced simultaneously, the prior absence of color is also necessarily a preceding factor fixed to the odor, just like the prior absence of odor.

The sense is: why is the prior absence of odor not considered "otherwise established" (anyathāsiddha) by the very prior absence of color, which is necessarily postulated? Regarding the phrase "that which is the causality": in the case of odor not produced by heat (*apākaja-gandha*), the causality for odor is postulated for the prior absence of odor itself, and not for the prior absence of color; therefore... [end of fragment] Rāmarudrī.

The point is that the prior non-existence of smell (*gandhaprāgabhāva*) is not established otherwise by the prior non-existence of color (*rūpaprāgabhāva*) in the case of a smell produced by baking (*pākaja*). Regarding the phrase "due to heaviness, etc.": this is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*). It means that the property of being a staff (*daṇḍatva*), etc., is the delimitor of the status of being an invariably antecedent factor (*niyatapūrvavartitāvacchedaka*) with respect to [the production of] a jar delimited by the universal of jar-ness (*ghaṭatva*). This too is an elliptical indication.

Causality is defined as the property that delimits the status of being an invariably antecedent factor with respect to a jar-ness-delimited effect; this is restricted to the stick-ness (daṇḍatva) and so forth, due to parsimony of hypothesis (kalpanālāghava). It is not, however, such a property as substantiality (dravyatva), because that would involve a complexity of hypothesis (kalpanāgaurava). To explain: [if it were substantiality,] there would be an over-extension of the property of substantiality as the delimiter of the status of being an invariably antecedent factor.

If [the causal capacity] were of the nature of being the cause of a jar, then a relation consisting of a causal capacity qualified by being determined by a jar would have to be postulated in infinite substances such as jars; if [the causal capacity] were of the nature of the stick-ness, then it would reside in the stick alone; if it were of the nature of the stick itself, then it would reside in the stick alone.
Thus it is said in the *Rāmarudrī*:
"It should also be observed that there is parsimony of hypothesis (*kalpanālāghava*) regarding the nature of the staff (*daṇḍatva*) in comparison to the nature of substance (*dravyatva*)."

Regarding the phrase "of the indefinite donkey and so forth": although this is redundant— since the term "indefinite" (*niyata*) was previously stated in order to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to the donkey, which is not otherwise established (*ananyathāsiddha*) with respect to that which is delimited by potness (*ghaṭatvāvacchinna*)— nevertheless, [the point remains that] it is by means of those very antecedents established elsewhere as being invariably prior (*niyatapūrvavartin*)...

The fifth type of extraneous relation (*anyathāsiddhi*), as defined by the ancients, is that which is co-existent with the effect and is established otherwise; this does not apply to a donkey in relation to a jar delimited by the property of "jar-ness" (*ghaṭatva*),
because [the production of the jar] is already accounted for by other factors established as its necessary antecedents elsewhere than in the jar itself.

Having established that the donkey is not "unconditionally established" (ananyathāsiddha) with respect to the jar by means of the formulation "because the production of a jar is impossible [from it]," the author stated the purposefulness of the term "niyata" (invariable). Now, however, the author [proceeds] with what is further: "Moreover, whatever else may exist that is invariably and necessarily antecedent..."

Thus, because the fifth type of "otherwise-established" (*anyathāsiddhi*) has been defined in this way, one might raise the objection that even a donkey is "otherwise-established" with respect to a jar delimited by the property of being a jar (*ghaṭatva-avacchinna*), and therefore [the definition] is redundant; it should be understood that the preceding statement is repeated here precisely to resolve such a doubt.
By the phrase "of donkeys, etc.," the inclusion of jars and so forth is intended.

By the phrase "invariably, etc.," the inclusion of being a prior entity (pūrvavartitva) is intended. Thus, since even the property of jar-ness (ghaṭatva) is a pervader with respect to a jar, the inclusion of being a prior entity is introduced in order to exclude over-extension (ativyāpti) in that case.

This is the intended meaning (*bhāva*). However, the meaning of "the state of possessing a property that is not a delimiting factor for the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) of an absence residing in the locus of the jar, as delimited by the moment immediately preceding the jar, with respect to the two petals joined together" should be understood as follows, according to Rāmarudrī. [The phrase] "by the absence of one" has already been explained. [The phrase] "in the absence of the object to be apprehended" (*grāhyābhāve*)...

The meaning is that the nature of negative deviation (vyatireka-vyabhicāra) consists precisely in the fact that the property intended to be the delimiting condition of causality (*kāraṇatāvacchedaka*) is itself the delimiting condition of the counterpositiveness (*pratiyogitāvacchedakatva*) of an absence that is co-located with the effect (*kārya-samānādhikaraṇa*). Regarding the term "positive deviation" (*anvaya-vyabhicāra*): [it refers to the case where the effect occurs even in the absence of the cause].
The sense is that even if a pervader (vyāpaka) exists in a larger locus, its status as a pervader is not lost.

"Due to the cognition of being otherwise established" (anyathāsiddhatva): the sense is that the cognition of the concomitant deviation (anvaya-vyabhicāra) acts as an inhibitor specifically with respect to the cognition of the factor of "not being otherwise established" (ananyathāsiddhatva), which constitutes a part of the definition of causality.

Regarding the phrase "as that particular individuality" (*tadvyaktitvena*): because the property of being an absence whose counterpositiveness is delimited by the relation of spatial qualification (*daiśika-viśeṣaṇatā*) and delimited by the universal of "jewel-ness" (*maṇitva*) is more cumbersome than the particularity residing in the absence of the jewel (*maṇyabhāva*), it is a superfluous factor (*anyathāsiddha*).

The point is this: since "simplicity" (lāghava) ultimately amounts to being the non-qualifier of the counter-correlate of the counterfactual (anyathāsiddhi-anirūpakatva), it follows that the property of being that specific individuality (tadvyaktitva) residing in the absence [of the obstructor]—provided it is the non-qualifier of the counterfactual—is the delimitor of its status as an invariably antecedent factor (niyatapūrvavartitāvacchedakatva). One might object: "Let it be that the absence of the obstructor is a cause by virtue of that specific individuality; what is lost for us?"

It must be stated that this would entail the undesirable consequence of abolishing the causality of the absence of a jewel (*maṇyabhāva*) and so forth with respect to burning and other effects—a causality that is accepted by all disputants. This is the intended meaning.
However, it should be observed that, according to the author’s own view, the only recourse here is the acceptance of the very consequence as being desired (*iṣṭāpatti*). Now, [an objection]:...

The nature of being a cause (kāraṇatva) as previously described need not be accepted; rather, one must accept that for whatever property-qualified entity there is no conventional usage of "causality," the causality belongs precisely to a property distinct from those. Therefore, the aforementioned fault does not apply; to this he says: "Where... (yatra).

The meaning is "delimited by a property" (*dharma*). The phrase "possessing a collection of differences" (*bhedakūṭavatva*) also has as its meaning simply "possessing a property that possesses a collection of differences. Therefore, there is no deficiency even if the difference delimited by that particularity (*tadvyaktitva*) is absent in that which is delimited by the state of being an absence of an inhibitor (*pratibandhakābhāvatva*). [This is stated] by the Omniscient One himself.

The meaning is that it is impossible for people like us to have knowledge of all the properties distinct from the delimitors of causality (*kāraṇatāvacchedaka*) in their respective individualities (*tattadvyaktitva*). Now, [one might object]: "If there is no linguistic usage of 'causality' with respect to that which is delimited by a particular property, then [the definition] is qualified by the effect in question through the relation of being the collection of the absences of those respective individuals."

If it is stated that causality is simply the state of possessing that property (dharma), this fault does not arise; for since the knowledge of a relation is not a cause for a qualified cognition (*viśiṣṭabuddhi*), even those individual particulars (*vyakti*) that were not previously present may appear as constituents of the relation.

He dispels the doubt regarding the absence of sublation and so forth with the words "tatadvyakti" (of each individual instance). The word "tasya" (of that) means "of such a collection of differences. The word "sarvadā" (always) [is used] because, in some cases—such as with a staff and the like—one must rely on the perception of the causal status of a jar; thus, regarding that causal status...

The meaning is that since fitness (*yogyatva*) must be admitted, whenever the perception of a staff occurs, there would necessarily follow the perception of the causality residing in that [staff] with respect to the jar. However, in our own view,
since causality consists in pervasion (*vyāpakatā*), and in the cognition of that pervasion...

The point is that this undesirable consequence does not arise because the knowledge of concomitance (*sahacārajñāna*) and the absence of the knowledge of deviation (*vyabhicārajñānābhāva*) serve as the causes [of the inference], and thus there is a delay due to them. "Its manifester" (*tadvyañjaka*) means the object of the perception that generates the perception of the causal capacity (*kāraṇatā*).
The phrase "prior to the apprehension of the causality of such knowledge of the property" and so forth [is used]. Now, one might object:

even if the knowledge of the property is required for the sake of knowing its causality, it is not possible for that [knowledge] to be of the nature of causality itself, because the aforementioned defect remains as it was. Anticipating this objection, he says: "Let it be."
Or rather [it is not so], because the postulation of a distinct category (*padārthāntara*) would involve unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*); this is the intended meaning.

Now, if the nature of being a staff (*daṇḍatva*) were identical with causality (*kāraṇatā*), then whenever there is a perception of the staff, there would necessarily follow a perception of the causality of the jar, since the property of being a staff (*daṇḍatva*) is present whenever there is sensory contact with the staff.
He dispels the doubt that [the definition] is necessarily required by stating: "by way of being related to effects such as a jar.
This means: "by way of being defined by a jar and so forth. Regarding the word "effect" (kārya): it refers to the positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) with the effect.
The absence of the effect, which has the effect as its counter-positive and whose relation is the effect; the state of being prior to the time of that locus;
the state of being the counter-positive of the destruction residing in that [locus]; and the state of possessing positive and negative concomitance occurring at such a prior time.
— Rāmarudrī.
It is the state of being the counter-positive of a prior absence residing in that [locus], while simultaneously being the counter-positive of a relation residing in that [locus].
This is because, while it is the counter-positive of a relation existing at a time prior to the time of the jar's relation [to its locus],
it is also the counter-positive of a prior absence existing at a time prior to the time of the jar's prior absence.

The stick and other such factors possess causality with respect to the jar. In this context, [causality] consists in being prior to the time of the effect's presence, or being the counter-positive of a destruction that pervades such a time. By this definition, there is no contingency of a thing being its own cause. However, being prior to the time of the effect's absence is not of that nature.
This is because there is no established instance of a time that is both non-pervasive of the time of the prior absence of a jar and a counter-positive of its own destruction;

rather, [the definition] consists simply in being the counter-positive of a destruction residing in such a time. It should be understood, however, that the inclusion of the negative (vyatireka) component is intended to exclude things such as the nature of a staff (daṇḍatva) or the ether (ākāśa) from being considered causes.

Regarding the phrase "in the self, etc.": the sense is that, because the term *vyatireka* (absence) must necessarily be taken as referring to *prāgabhāva* (prior non-existence) in order to exclude [the presence of] stickness and so forth, [the definition would fail]. This is also an elliptical indication [of other points]: namely, that at the time preceding the connection with the effect, there is the state of not being a locus for the prior non-existence of the time that is the locus of the prior non-existence of the effect.

Even if the inclusion of a qualification (viśe�ṣaṇa) makes it possible to exclude those factors that precede [the effect] but are separated from it by an interval, the resulting attribution of causality to things such as a staff, a color, or a donkey remains impossible to avoid. Likewise,
in the case of prior non-existence (prāgabhāva), there is no [factor] whatsoever that possesses the property of being temporally prior to the prior non-existence of the effect.
It should also be observed that prior non-existence (prāgabhāva) is useless [as a definition], since it does not serve to exclude [the undesired]. || 19 || 20 ||

21 || 22 || "There is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in the case of substance (*dravya*). Thus, the term "genus" (*jāti*) is intended precisely to capture both the state of being a locus (*vṛttimatva*) and the state of residing (*vṛttitva*) by way of inherence (*samavāya*).
Therefore, the meaning is that even if "either-ness" (*anyataratva*) does not possess these properties, it is not redundant. 23 ||
The phrase "by means of relations such as inherence" (*samavāyādi-sambandhena*) is explained by the expression "being the substratum of all" (*sarvādhāratā*) and so forth;
for by the word "etc. (*ādi*), it is possible to include the temporal relation (*kālika*) as well. Regarding the phrase "other than the temporal relation":
here, the term "temporal" (*kālika*) is also indicative of spatial qualification (*dig-viśeṣaṇatā*), since that too [is included].

It should be understood that this is because [the category of substance] serves as the basis for everything. To exclude the spatial objectness (*daiśika-viṣayatā*), he says "temporal" (*kālika*). Now, although the word "here" (*iha*) in the phrase "dependence is stated here" in the root-text refers to the previously mentioned substance, [it does not imply] the status of being a substance distinct from eternal substances.

The term "lakṣyatāvacchedaka" (the delimitor of the definiendum) is thus obtained; and so, since the property of being dependent (*āśritatva*) exists even in qualities (*guṇa*) and the like, there arises the suspicion of over-extension (*ativyāpti*). He dispels this doubt with the word "atra" (here). Thus, the meaning of "iha" (here) is simply "in the established doctrine of Nyāya. However, in the view of the Vedāntins...

It should be understood that this [definition] is stated to dispel the suspicion of non-pervasion (*avyāpti*) regarding eternal knowledge (*nityajñāna*), since it is accepted as being without a substratum (*anāśrita*). As for the phrase "even of an atom":
since only conjunction (*saṃyoga*) which prevents falling is the regulator of existence (*vṛtti-niyāmaka*) in the case of space (*gagana*) and so forth...
Since falling would otherwise be impossible in the absence of gravity,

even if one does not postulate that conjunction with it (the earth) acts as an obstacle to falling, it is nevertheless necessary that, because the atoms of earth and water possess gravity, their conjunction with a location such as the ground must act as an obstacle to falling.

The point is that even for the atoms of earth and so forth, conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is indeed a regulator of occurrence (*vṛttiniyāmaka*). Regarding the phrase "because it is not a regulator of occurrence": since gravity produced by action (*janya-gurutva*) or intense gravity (*prakṛṣṭa-gurutva*) is the cause of falling, and because falling is impossible for an atom precisely due to the absence of such [gravity], [conjunction is not required].

The reason is that there is no evidence for the conjunction with that [ether] being a preventer of falling; otherwise, in the absence of preventers such as air and so forth, all atoms would necessarily fall downwards—this is the intended meaning. Regarding the phrase "at this time":

And thus, the sense is that the word *tu* is used to indicate the exclusion of other [meanings] that possess a common property distinct from substance (*dravya*). || 14 || Regarding "the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is action (*kriyā*)," the remainder [of the explanation] is: "For the meaning of the verbal root is to be known as action; it is designated as 'being' (*bhāva*)," according to the verse of Harikārika.

Regarding the phrase "karmavatvam iti": the point is that, in the present context, the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is not the action (*kriyā*), but rather the object (*karman*) itself. One might mistakenly think that "possessing momentum" (*vega-vattva*) means "having a state similar to momentum"—an interpretation based on the etymology "the state of that which has momentum, like momentum. [This is the error being addressed.]

To refute this, he says: "the state of being connected with velocity. However, the objection raised in the root text by the words "but not" (*na tu na*) and so forth—namely, that there is an over-narrow definition (*avyāpti*) where priority and posteriority do not arise—is inappropriate;
for, just as with other qualities, it is possible for these two to arise everywhere at the very second moment of their production, especially since momentary entities [do not persist].
He dispels the doubt that [the author] does not accept [this definition] by stating "of those produced by direction. In the phrase "thus [arises] relative cognition" (*ity apekṣābuddhiḥ*),
the word *iti* has the sense of "in this manner," thereby including the cognition "this is distant from that."
Therefore, there is no harm in the fact that the cognition of proximity is not a cause for the apprehension of "otherness" (*paratva*);

the same should be understood in subsequent cases as well. Although, according to the verse of the Teacher (Vācaspati Miśra), "The Omniscient and Immutable One is to be established from the sentence and from the specific number," duality exists in atoms—

It must necessarily be admitted that [priority and posteriority] are produced by God’s relative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*); and thus, the production of priority and posteriority everywhere through an eternal relative cognition is indeed possible. Nevertheless, although the duality of atoms is necessary for the sake of otherwise explaining the dimension of the dyad (*dvyaṇuka*), [the following applies].

The intention is that since the cognition of priority and posteriority is not established by experience in such jars and the like, there is a lack of evidence for priority and posteriority in such jars; therefore, only a produced relative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*) is the cause of priority and posteriority. Alternatively:
Since the conjunction with the mass of space (*dikpiṇḍa*) is also a cause of priority (*paratva*) and posteriority (*aparatva*),
the intended meaning is that even in the case of such a jar whose destruction occurs in the third moment, [the quality] would be non-pervasive (*avyāpti*).
This is because at the very moment of the production of priority and posteriority, their production becomes impossible due to the destruction of the substratum (*āśraya*).

[The term] "bhāvaḥ" [is used]. Regarding the phrase "also by way of being other than substanceness" (*dravyatvānyatvena*): in reality, however, what is intended here is simply "being pervaded by substanceness," which, due to parsimony (*lāghavāt*), means "subsisting in a locus smaller than that of substanceness.

And this consists in being the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) of the counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) of a difference that is co-locative with substanceness; it does not consist in substanceness itself.

Thus, there is no possibility of over-extension (*ativyāpti*) by including [the aforementioned]. Nor should one suspect that over-extension occurs precisely because qualities such as *guṇatva* (the state of being a quality) also possess that same nature; for we consider it correct to hold that these lack co-occurrence (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with priority (*paratva*) and posteriority (*aparatva*). Regarding the phrase "inferior" (*apakṛṣṭa*), [it refers to] the dimension (*parimāṇa*) of an atom (*paramāṇu*).

Anticipating the objection that there might be an over-narrow application (*avyāpti*) because there is no absence of being drawn away from somewhere, he says: "occurring in non-omnipresent [substances]" (*avibhu-vṛtti*).

However, having accepted a difference in genus (*vaijātya*) regarding conjunction occurring in non-omnipresent [substances], such a heterogeneous conjunction [is the cause] in action not produced by velocity (*vega*) and so forth.

Even if one accepts that [space] is a cause, since it is possible to exclude action from an all-pervading entity (*vibhu*), the proof of the genus *mūrtatva* (corporeality) as the delimitor of the status of being an inherent cause of action (*kriyā-samavāyi-kāraṇatāvacchedaka*) is not a decisive factor; thus, with the intention of indicating this lack of finality, he says: "some say."

Regarding the phrase "And that" (*tac ceti*): he says "And that" in order to dispel the doubt that the word "and" (*ca*) would be redundant because there is no other distinct object to be conjoined by it. He says "The word 'and' has the sense of 'but'" (*castvarthaḥ*) in order to dispel the doubt that the word "and" would be redundant because there is no other distinct object to be conjoined;
for by the sense of "but" (*tu*) in the phrase "and [it is] by this," the inherence of the all-pervasive dimension (*vibhu-parimāṇa*) in earth and the other elements is [distinguished].

The sense is that it is not redundant because it serves to exclude [other possibilities]. Regarding "in time, etc.": the sense is that omnipresence—characterized by the possession of motion and being the object of all corporeal actions—is impossible in the case of time and so forth, which are devoid of action.
Now, having stated that "supreme magnitude" (*paramamahattvatva*) is a genus (*jāti*), [the author] of its...

In the root text, another alternative has been followed: that [the nature of dimension] is "dimensionality that is not a locus of diminution," because there is no evidence proving it to be a genus (*jāti*) therein due to its not being delimited by causality and so forth.
However, that is incorrect, because such a genus could be perceived in the dimensions residing in the self (*ātman*).

He dispels the objection that "since there exists perception itself as its means of proof" by stating "I," and so forth. Regarding the term "great" (*mahān*), [the word] "supreme" (*parama*) is supplied; thus, even though "supreme greatness" (*paramamahattvatva*) is not the object of the cognition "great," there is no deficiency.

"Even though," and so forth. Furthermore, although there is no diminution in the dimension of an atom relative to other atomic dimensions, there certainly is a diminution relative to the atoms of jars and the like,
because of the difference between being and not being established by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
It must be said that this is because increase and decrease are possible even for those two [length and breadth].
For it is a rule that the increase and decrease residing in atoms are restricted by their own kind of dimension to being limited by a dimension of the same class; otherwise, how could this be?

The meaning is that in the case of magnitude (*vibhuparimāṇa*), there is no diminution relative to the magnitude of an atom (*paramāṇuparimāṇa*), because both [magnitude and atomicity] can possess increase and diminution based on their being or not being applicable to action; "increase" and "diminution" are specific universals (*jāti*) residing in number, as in "this is superior to that."
It should be understood that by the force of such cognitions, even these two [the large and the minute] are admitted to have limits.

Regarding "largeness and minuteness": thus, although the dimension of an atom possesses the property of not being a locus of further diminution (*apakarṣānāśrayatva*), it does not possess "supreme largeness" (*paramamahattva*) precisely because it lacks the nature of largeness (*mahattvatva*).
[The word] "existence" [is used]. Regarding the phrase "the term 'external'": externality should be understood as nothing other than being distinct from the mind.
"Belonging to the same class as the object of apprehension" means possessing a genus that is the object of ordinary perception produced by the external sense organs.
This is because, in the case of the perception of conjunction, there must be perception of all its substrata, and that [perception of all substrata] is absent here.

Since the conjunction with time is not an object of perception, it is necessary to pursue the definition up to the class [of perceptible objects]. Furthermore, the qualification "belonging to the same class as the apprehended" is essential; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of over-narrowness (*avyāpti*) regarding the color of atoms and the like, because those are not perceptible.
The state [of being]. "It will be stated" refers to the remaining portion of the verse beginning with "the group of six starting with intellect" (*buddhyādi-ṣaṭkam*).

Regarding the phrase "taking substance-ness (*dravyatva*) as the basis": although it will be stated later that the nature of a specific quality (*viśeṣaguṇatva*) is simply being any one of the [specific qualities] such as color (*rūpa*) and so forth, and in that case, there is no [separate category of] "specific-ness" (*viśeṣatva*) or "quality-ness" (*guṇatva*)...

Nevertheless, in this context, "particularity" (*viśeṣatva*) is intended as being distinct from general qualities (*sāmānyaguṇa*), such that "particular quality-ness" (*viśe�ṣaguṇatva*) is simply the state of being a quality (*guṇatva*) accompanied by that [distinction]. With this intention, it was stated that there would be an over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to substance-ness (*dravyatva*) and so forth, because substance-ness is also distinct from general qualities. And even so, it is not the case that...

It should not be argued that there is no over-extension (atiprasaṅga) by taking "substantiality" (dravyatva), precisely because substantiality lacks any genus (jāti) perceptible by the external sense organs;
for the term "substantiality" signifies that which is not inherent in anything other than substance, and since action (kriyā) also possesses this property,
the intended meaning [of the definition] is clearly the over-extension of the definition to the mind (manas) by taking action as the basis.

The sense is that, because "being any one of several" (anyatamatva)—which consists of the absence whose counter-correlativity is delimited by a collection of differences—is cumbersome, it is more appropriate for the definition to consist of "the state of being a quality" (guṇatva) itself, qualified by the possession of a collection of differences from general qualities.
Regarding the phrase "of the eye, etc.": although the inherence in the self conjoined with the eye [is a cause] in respect to cognition...
Because [the object] exists [in the eye], and because there is no worldly sense-contact [there], this is highly inconsistent; nevertheless,

it is necessary that only the inherence in what is conjoined with the eye and is fit [to be perceived] constitutes the sense-contact, otherwise, at the time of the eye's conjunction with an atom, there would follow the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of perceiving the "substance-ness" (*dravyatva*) and other properties inherent in that [atom].
The sense is that because the self lacks the requisite capacity, there is no ordinary sensory contact (*laukika-saṃnikarṣa*) with respect to knowledge.

Regarding the phrase "in [the case of] magnitude" (*mahattve*): one might raise the objection that since the perception of color and so forth occurs in a jar even in the absence of magnitude, the perception of color should likewise occur in an atom even in the absence of magnitude. To address this doubt:
He sets it aside with the words "laukika" (worldly) and so on. Regarding the phrase "because of the unsuitability for apprehension":

the sense is that since, with respect to worldly perception produced by the external senses, the cause is precisely the quality of manifested color (*udbhūtarūpatva*), [the atom] possesses the status of being suitable because it possesses the property that delimits the causal capacity (*kāraṇatāvacchedakadharma*). [Commentary: Rāmarudrī: Now, an objection... [text resumes]... nanu.
The fitness for being an object of ordinary external sensory perception is not included in the definition;
rather,
it is simply the possession of a genus that is co-extensive with, but narrower than, the quality-ness (guṇatva) residing in objects of ordinary external sensory perception.

Furthermore, since the genus "being of such a nature" (tathāvidharūpatva) and so forth—which constitutes the definition—is present even in the form of the eye and other [senses], there is no lack of pervasion (avyāpti) regarding the eye and so on; because of this underlying dissatisfaction, he says: "And because of parsimony" (lāghavāt).
Or rather, as for the phrase "or else": [one might object] that in this alternative, non-residence in the self (ātmāvṛttitva) must be by way of inherence (samavāyena).
It is more appropriate to state that [the definition of a particularity] consists simply in possessing a property that does not delimit its occurrence in the self; otherwise,

if it were defined as being distinct from what occurs in the self, there would be the consequence of unnecessary complexity (gaurava) due to the inclusion of "particularity" (viśeṣatva), which is itself a collection of distinctions from general qualities (sāmānyaguṇabheda).

In this way, even without the inclusion of "particularity" (*viśeṣatva*), the avoidance of over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to time and so forth is possible, because time and the like do not possess such a property as inhering in conjunction (*saṃyoga*).
To dispel the doubt that the inclusion of "particularity" is therefore useless, [the author] proceeds to its inclusion...
He states another purpose with the words "and here" (*atra ca*). The phrase "by means of inherence" (*samavāyena*) is to be understood as completing the sense of "is to be known" (*bodhyam*).

The underlying intention is that otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to time and space—which possess touch—due to their being related by temporal and spatial qualification (*kālika-dikkṛta-viśeṣaṇatā*). || 26 ||

Regarding the phrase "pervaded by substanceness" (*dravyatvavyāpya*): although it might be argued that since "substanceness" itself is also pervaded by "substanceness," the previously mentioned fault remains as it was, nevertheless, one should keep in mind that the same reasoning applied earlier should be followed here as well; therefore, no fault whatsoever exists. Regarding the phrase "for the sake of excluding [the definition from] jars and the like" (*ghaṭādivyāvṛttyai*). Rāmarudrī.
Since it will be stated later that "possessing a momentary specific quality" constitutes a different definition,

the purpose [of the current definition] is to exclude the over-extension (*ativyāpti*) of "possessing a specific quality that is the counter-positive of its own destruction" to things such as a jar; for even now, that form of a jar which exists in the third moment—

It should not be argued that the defect of over-extension (*ativyāpti*) remains there, because it will be addressed later. "Occurring in the second moment" means occurring in its own second moment. And this [definition] applies to cases other than those involving *apekṣābuddhi* (relational cognition).

In this context, however, it should be understood that one must simply say "occurring at the third moment. In reality, the phrase "occurring immediately after itself" (*svottaravṛti*) in the root text means "occurring immediately following [itself]" (*svāvyavahitottaravartin*).
Being immediately subsequent is defined as being subsequent to its own specific quality (*viśeṣaguṇa*), while not being subsequent to any other specific quality occurring after itself.

It should be understood that "being posterior to itself" (*svottaratva*)—which consists in being the counter-positive of a prior absence (*prāgabhāva*) residing in itself—is capable of encompassing both [the antecedent and the subsequent] through a single expression. Furthermore, since "selfhood" (*svatva*) lacks a commonality (*ananugata*), the causal relation must rest upon each specific individual instance (*vyakti*); thus, with respect to the destruction of a particular instance, it occurs by virtue of that very instance's identity (*tattadvyaktitvena*).

With the intention that causality would be untenable because properties such as "occurring in its own second moment" do not serve to differentiate [causes], and because it would result in an infinite regress of cause-and-effect relations leading to excessive complexity (gaurava), he says: "And here... [The definition is: "being immediately prior," which means:
while being the non-locus of the antecedent absence of the locus of its own antecedent absence.

The state of being the locus of one's own prior non-existence (*svaprāgabhāvādhikaraṇatva*) constitutes immediate antecedence (*avyavahitapūrvatva*). In this context, the inclusion of "co-occurrence in the same locus" (*svasāmānādhikaraṇya*) is for the purpose of precluding the destruction [of the object] in the third moment by means of a cognition belonging to another person that arises in the second moment following the enumerative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*). This refers to the second moment of the enumerative cognition.
And the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) is that there is no production of a specific quality (*viśeṣaguṇa*) suitable for a *tatpuruṣa* [body].

The inclusion of the second relation is for the purpose of precluding the momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*) of cognition (*jñāna*) and so forth. "There is no deviation" (*na vyabhicāraḥ*) means there is no positive deviation (*anvaya-vyabhicāra*). Now, as for suitability (*yogyatva*)...

To dispel the doubt that, because indeterminate perception (*nirvikalpaka*) has the nature of being an object of worldly perception (*laukikapratyakṣa*), it would not be destroyed by subsequent cognitions and the like, he defines its "fitness" (*yogyatā*)—saying "and fitness... Out of parsimony (*lāghava*), he says "transcendental" (*atīndriya*). [This concludes] the section on the nature of indeterminate perception (*nirvikalpakatva*). Rāmarudrī.
However, it is not a genus (*jāti*), because the nature of non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpakatva*) consists precisely in being a cognition devoid of qualifiers;
the point is that "cognition-ness" (*jñānatva*) is not supersensible (*atīndriya*). Regarding the phrase "destruction of color, etc.":
here the term "deviation" (*vyabhicāra*) refers to negative deviation (*vyatireka-vyabhicāra*), given the presence of color.

Because there is no possibility of a deviation from the positive concomitance (*anvaya-vyabhicāra*) due to the non-arising of another form [of the same substance], so it is in the subsequent cases as well. One should understand that there is a deviation [in the argument] because the conjunction with space (*gagana*) residing in a jar is neither destroyed nor produced by the color and other qualities produced by baking (*pākaja*). Regarding the phrase "of those residing in different loci" (*vyadhikaraṇānām*): this moreover...

It has been stated, in accordance with the actual nature of things, that only qualities residing in the same substratum (*samānādhikaraṇa*) possess the power to destroy [a quality]; for even if sound were destroyed by a desire residing in a different substratum (*vyadhikaraṇecchā*), it would still be possible to maintain the desired conclusion by establishing that sound persists for two moments. However, our own position alone is correct.

The term "exclusion" (vyāvṛtti) is to be understood as such. "By desire and so forth arising at the time of production" means by desire and so forth produced in the immediately preceding moment. Although it would have been more appropriate to state that a thing cannot be its own destroyer, nevertheless—

It should be understood that this far-reaching pursuit was undertaken because "immediately preceding existence" (*svāvyavahita-pūrvavartitva*) is cumbersome; therefore, by substituting it with "being different from itself" (*svabhinnatva*), it is possible to prevent a thing from being its own destroyer.
This [principle] applies even to the destruction of enumerative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*).

Because if the individuals of the non-conceptual cognition of duality produced in the third moment were causes by virtue of their respective individual natures (*tattadvyaktitva*), there would be an infinite regress of cause-and-effect relations (*anantakāryakāraṇabhāva*), resulting in excessive complexity (*gaurava*); therefore, it is possible to assert that they possess a single causal nature (*ekakāraṇatā*).
With the intention that it would be improper to accept [such] respectability, he says: "But of the enumerative cognition (apekṣābuddhi)," etc.

[The point is: at a single moment, because various individual instances of specific qualities perish, one must postulate that each such instance is a cause for the destruction of its respective individual instance by virtue of being that specific instance.
Since this [explanation] accomplishes a greater number of causal relations,

it is simpler to hold that the causality for the destruction of a particular quality of an all-pervading substance arising at a specific moment consists simply in being a quality characterized by existing in the moment immediately following that moment.

With the intention that it is appropriate to say this, he says: "arisen at this very moment. [Objection: But in this way, even the *apekṣābuddhi* (the enumerative cognition) would face destruction by a quality existing in its own second moment; and thus, if the *apekṣābuddhi* were destroyed at the very moment of the non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpaka*) of duality, then duality would be destroyed in the fourth moment due to the absence of its object, and consequently, at that moment—
Because the perception of duality as qualified [by its substratum] would otherwise be untenable, he says: "dependent on the cognition," and so forth.
He refers to it as the "specific causal complex" (*viśeṣasāmagrī*). Thus, it is precisely when accompanied by this specific causal complex that—[as stated in the Rāmarudrī].

The point is this: although the general causal complex (*sāmānyasāmagrī*) exists because it is the producer of the effect, the destruction of the relative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*) does not occur in the third moment due to the absence of the specific causes in the form of the perception of duality (*dvitvapratyakṣa*). Now, if this is so, then in the first alternative (*kalpa*), immediately after that cognition...

Liberation would be impossible because, following such knowledge, there is no production of cognition and so forth within that self, which implies its destruction; furthermore, if it were to destroy itself by virtue of being that very individual instance, it would follow that it is momentary. And if, even after that [knowledge], there were the production of conjunctions with jars and other objects therein—

That very [moment] is called the destroyer; nevertheless, if one accepts the production of a quality in the second moment following the final direct realization of the Self— which arose in the third moment prior to the great dissolution— then, by not admitting that qualities are momentary, [the quality would persist] into the third moment.

Since a great dissolution (mahāpralaya) is impossible [if all karma were destroyed], that which could cause its destruction is indeed difficult to find. Nor should it be argued that, because the great dissolution would be impossible due to the absence of a cause for the destruction of all unseen merit and demerit (adṛṣṭa) by the final self-realization, [the doctrine is untenable]; for, in accordance with the occurrence of a great dissolution, that very moment [of realization]— [...is what effects the destruction.]
Because it is accepted that [the merit] which produces that [effect] acts as an obstacle when its own destruction occurs, he says:

"But the final cognition and so forth... Here, by the phrase "they say," the excessive complexity resulting from an infinite number of causal relations is indicated. Regarding the phrase "because of being all-pervasive": [this refers to] God's...

The meaning is that, due to the separation from the body, it is impossible for [the cognition] to be delimited by that [body]. (Rāmarudrī) "There is no defect" means there is no impossibility. He states the purpose of the phrase "occurring during four moments"—namely, "and including the end of the occurrence"—by [pointing out] that otherwise, taking "cognition-ness" (*jñānatva*) as the basis, there would be no inclusion of the self (*ātman*).
The occurrence in the third moment has been disregarded solely because the definition can be satisfied by taking "desire-ness" (icchātva) as the basis;
thus it is indicated that one could also say [the definition applies] to that which exists for three moments.

"By the intention that it has the meaning exactly as it was heard" means: by the intention that it has the meaning of being qualified by a body through the relation of possessing knowledge and so forth delimited by itself. || 27 || [Rāmarudrī] He says "the state of being subject to falling" in order to remove the deficiency of the root text. This is to be understood as [the object of the word] "to be known."

The similarity between earth and water, and so forth, has been stated. He defines the nature of falling as "gravity" (*gurutva*). Now, since atoms would otherwise never fall, it must be admitted that only an intense degree of gravity (*prakṛṣṭa-gurutva*) serves as the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyi-kāraṇa*) of falling.

It should not be argued that there is an over-narrow definition (*avyāpti*) because falling is impossible in the case of an atom due to the absence of such [gravity] therein; for the intended meaning is "possessing a genus subordinate to substancehood (*dravyatvavyāpyajāti*) that resides in that which possesses falling. However, even so, the usage "the meteor falls" (*ulkā patati*) would be untenable.

Because falling is impossible for a meteor, which consists of light, due to the absence of gravity, he says "ulkā" (meteor). Regarding the term "lākṣaṇika," it refers to the meaning of the verbal root *gam* and so forth.
With the intention of [expressing] lightness, he says "vastutastu" (but in reality). [The phrase] "jātiviśeṣa eva" (only a particular genus) [is used].
The point is that its establishment occurs precisely through its being the delimitor (*avacchedaka*) of the state of being produced by gravity (*gurutvajanyatā*). || 28 || Now, [one might object]:
"In the root-text it was stated: 'That which is the similarity (*sādharmya*) of one thing is the dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) of the other.'"

To dispel the objection that a general statement regarding the common properties (*sādharmya*) of the seven categories— such as their being objects of knowledge (*jñeyatva*) and so forth— is improper because there is no established "other" (i.e., nothing outside the seven categories) from which they could be distinguished by dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*), he states "Now then" (*nanu*) and so on, completing the argument in the *Muktāvalī* by excluding "being an object of knowledge" and the like.

29 || Regarding the verse beginning with "prācīnaślokam": this verse is seen in some manuscripts of the *Kāvalī* commentary; it should be understood as an interpolation, because of its incompatibility with this [author's] own statement. Rāmarudrī: "Aikyataḥ" means "because of being of the same genus. By this, [the distinction between] space and time [is established].

There is no harm even if there is a difference in size and so forth, because that is not a determining factor. This is because, since the Lord's dimension is unproduced, although substance-ness is a cause for produced dimensions, it is not so for [the Lord's] own dimension.

The point is that it is impossible to establish the existence of dimension (*parimāṇa*) in God by means of the aforementioned inference, even when assisted by the favorable reasoning (*anukūlatarka*) consisting in the apprehension of such a causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*). [Objection: But surely, if substantiality (*dravyatva*) were to deviate from dimension, then it would not be unconditional (*nirupādhika*).

By means of the aforementioned inference, assisted by a favorable *tarka* (reductio ad absurdum), the proof of dimension (*parimāṇa*) in the Lord (*īśvara*) is indeed free from obstacles; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that dimension could not be established even for time and space (*kāla* and *diś*). Due to this underlying unease, [the author] states the "unestablished nature of the essence" (*svarūpāsiddhi*) in the aforementioned inference, beginning with the words "The Lord. For this very reason, according to the Vedāntins, [there is no dimension] in the Lord.

The sense is that even the dispute regarding [the self] being of the nature of self-luminous bliss becomes consistent. As for the phrase "it has been refuted": since, in accordance with common usage such as "form is distinct from the pot," the word *pṛthak* (distinct/separate) necessarily has the meaning of "different" (*bhinna*), it follows that this applies even in the case of "the pot is distinct from the cloth."

The point is that since [the distinction] is established by having that very [Brahman] as its object, such a cognition does not establish another quality in the form of separateness (*prthaktva*). This will become clear further on. [As it says:
"Brahman is eternal consciousness and bliss," and "The knower of the bliss of Brahman..."
The meaning is that the Goddess is established in eternal bliss, according to such scriptural passages as "She fears nothing whatsoever.

Regarding the term *saṃkhyā* (number): the meaning is that the Lord is established in eternal bliss, according to such scriptural passages as "Nārāyaṇa alone indeed existed. Regarding *saṃkhyā*: "Nārāyaṇa alone indeed existed... [and so forth].

The sense is that its establishment is through such scriptural passages as these. Regarding "number": the sense is that its establishment is through scriptural passages such as "Nārāyaṇa alone indeed was.
However, knowledge, desire, and effort are established solely by means of the inference of having an agent (sakartṛkatva) with respect to the earth.
This has been established above. Nor should it be argued that the Śruti passage, "smaller than the small, greater than the great," establishes even a spatial dimension (parimāṇa) for the Lord;
for since largeness and smallness are mutually contradictory, both cannot possibly coexist in one and the same entity. As for largeness...

The core intention is that, because [the Lord's] nature consists in being undivided by space and time, and because it is precisely His state of being the inner controller (*antaryāmin*) of all that must be stated in this context, [the atomicity of the soul is not intended here]. || 30 || 31 || 32 || 33 || 34 || Thus ends [the section] in the *Muktāvalīprakāśataraṅgiṇī* composed by the venerable Rāmarudra Bhaṭṭācārya.
First Wave. [Rāmarudrī]: Regarding the phrase "in time, etc. (kālādau):

the sense is that the causal efficiency delimited by the relation of identity—which is itself delimited by the effectness delimited by the property of being an effect residing in smell—is indeed present in time as well. Now, if one intends to specify the effectness delimited by the property of smell (gandhatva)...
This is not a fault; moreover, such an intention [to specify the relation] is necessary, otherwise,
even if one intends to specify that the effect-ness is delimited by the relation of inherence (*samavāya*),

one would still have to take into account the causality delimited by substantiality (*dravyatva*) as determined by the effect-ness delimited by the quality-ness (*guṇatva*) which is itself delimited by the relation of inherence residing in odor.

The word "etc. (*ādi*) has been employed with the intention that [the definition] would otherwise result in over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to water and so forth; it should be understood that by this, the inclusion of the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) which is of a different genus from the cause delimited by the nature of odor (*gandhatva*) is intended.
The phrase "existing in that which possesses odor" (*gandhavadvṛtti*) and so forth refers to the passage beginning with "merely the state of possessing odor" (*gandhavattvamātra*).

"Subsumed under substantiality (*dravyatva-vyāpya*)" means "subsisting in a locus smaller than that of substantiality. By this, since substantiality itself is also subsumed under substantiality, there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to water and so forth by taking that [substantiality] as the definition; the same should be understood for what follows. Regarding "no non-pervasion (*avyāpti*)," this is stated to exclude non-pervasion in the case of such a jar.

Since the previously mentioned state of possessing odor (*gandhavattva*) itself must be intended [as the definition], it would be more appropriate to state "being the inherent cause of odor" (*gandhasamavāyikāraṇatva*) as the definition for the sake of parsimony; nevertheless,

since such a capacity in the form of essential fitness (*svarūpayogyatā*) exists even in such a jar with respect to that which is delimited by earthness (*pṛthivītva*), [the definition would over-apply].

Because of the possibility of being endowed with [the universal] lakṣaṇa. Nor should it be argued that "being pervaded by substanceness" (dravyatvavyāpyatva) is simply the state of being a delimiting factor for the counter-correlativity of a difference residing in substance; for, just as in the case of causality, there would be the same complexity (gaurava) due to the inclusion therein of the restrictive element consisting in not being a delimiting factor for the counter-correlativity of an absence residing in that which possesses odor, as well as the element of non-redundancy (ananyathāsiddhatva). This is true here as well.

It is indicated that because the inclusion of "jāti" (universal), whose nature consists of being composed of properties such as eternality (*nityatva*), would result in an overly broad definition (*ativyāpti*) due to the lack of a decisive criterion for selection (*vinigamanāviraha*), its status as a definition is unavoidable. Thus, by taking "either-or-ness" (*anyataratva*) into account, the possibility of an overly broad definition does not arise.

Taking the duality of water and earth, [the term] *rāmarudrī* [is used]. It should be understood that the word "genus" (*jāti*) is included precisely to avoid over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to water. "By way of commonality with the unfit" means by way of having the unfit as its qualificandum (*viśeṣya*). The meaning of the third case-ending (*tṛtīyā*) is "distinctness" (*vaiśiṣṭya*).

The meaning is: "by virtue of its commonality with that," i.e., by virtue of its subsistence in unsuitable [entities] such as atoms (*paramāṇu*). Consequently, the universal *pṛthivītva* (earthness) is not established in an atom through perception;

rather, even there, the universal *pṛthivītva*, which serves as the delimiting factor for the causality of that [smell], is established solely through inference based on the effect in the form of smell (*gandha*), given the production of smell therein.
[The term] "bhāvaḥ" [refers to existence]. Regarding "niyatakāraṇa" (having a restricted cause): restriction with respect to the cause means precisely the exclusion from water and so forth.

Being "niyamya" (restricted) means possessing a property that delimits the effect-ness (*kāryatāvacchedakadharma*). Thus, if earth-ness were not the cause with respect to odor, its production might occur even in water and so forth at some time.

[This is] the state of affairs. Now, this contingency does not arise; for in the case of odor produced by cooking (*pākaja-gandha*), the conjunction with fire functions as the cause by way of being a conjunction with fire of a different class, whereas in the case of non-cooked odor, the cause is simply the odor of the constituent parts.

Since the production of odor in water and other substances is impossible precisely due to the absence of that [earth-element], one must admit that the specific universal (*vaijātya*) resides only in a conjunction whose relatum is earth; otherwise, because a single specific universal would be the delimiting factor for the production of color and so forth, it would follow that color and other qualities would be produced in water and the like as well. Nor is it the case that...
It should not be argued that the undesirable consequence does not arise there precisely because of the presence of an obstacle consisting of color;

for since the very property that delimits the production of another color also delimits the destruction of the previous color, it is the destruction itself that must be entailed. Out of dissatisfaction with this [position], he states his own view with the words "And thus... (tathāca).

The phrase "because of the rule regarding being the delimiting factor of effectness" means "because of the rule regarding being the delimiting factor of the effectness of an effect produced by an inherent cause. Consequently, even though the property of odor-ness (*gandhatva*) is the delimiting factor for being produced by a heterogeneous unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*), [the aforementioned rule remains intact].

There would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the non-establishment of "earth-ness" (*pṛthivītva*). The meaning is that the establishment of pervasion (*vyāpti*), however, occurs precisely through the observation of the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) between pot-ness (*ghaṭatva*) and the state of being a potsherd (*kapālatva*), and so forth.
Now, regarding the aforementioned pervasion:

Because there is an absence of proof due to the lack of a supporting *tarka* (reductio ad absurdum) for its existence, he presents another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) out of dissatisfaction [with the previous argument], beginning with "this" (*idam*). Regarding "distinct" (*vilakṣaṇā*): it is called "distinct" because color (*rūpa*) is neither destroyed nor produced through conjunction with light and so forth.
— Rāmarudrī.

Regarding the phrase "of being its own occurrence" (*svavṛtirūpatvasya*): since there is no evidence that "the nature of color" (*rūpatva*) has conjunction with fire as its counter-correlate (*pratiyogika*), the inclusion of "being its own occurrence" is made. This is because, even in the case of an indirect relation (*paraṃparā-sambandha*), the portion consisting of the specific qualifier itself possesses a counter-correlate.

The meaning is as follows: since a relation within a specific lineage is necessarily characterized by having a counter-correlative (*sapratyogika*), the inherence (*vṛtti*) of that [quality]—namely, its subsistence (*ādheyatā*)—is a counter-correlative of the conjunction with fire; thus, it is possible for its own subsistence as a form [of color] to have that [conjunction] as its counter-correlative.

"Residing in the earth which is its own inherent substratum" means: residing in that which is the relatum (*anuyogi*) of an inherence (*samavāya*) qualified by being the counter-correlate (*pratiyogika*) of a conjunction with a distinct kind of fire. Thus, there is no fault even if "earth-ness" (*pṛthivītva*) is not included.

The meaning is that [the author] does not accept that fire possesses the status of being the relatum (anuyogitva) of an inherence relation qualified by having as its counter-correlative (pratiyogika) a conjunction with fire. Regarding the word "fire" (*tejaḥ*):

the phrase "by way of being a conjunction with a heterogeneous fire" (*vijātīyatejaḥsaṃyogatvena*) is to be supplied. Consequently, there is no undesired consequence (*āpatti*) of odor occurring in water and so forth.
The core point is that [the author] accepts only conjunction (saṃyoga) residing in earth as being of a different genus (vaijātya).
As for the phrase "it has been refuted," the intended meaning is that even in the absence of such a causal relation (kāryakāraṇabhāva),
its existence is established precisely by its inclusion within the relational complex that delimits the capacity to destroy color (rūpanāśakatāvacchedaka-sambandha).

Regarding the phrase "by way of being earth": the root text’s claim that "because odor exists in stones and the like" is inconsistent, as there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to establish that [odor] therein. To dispel this doubt, Rāmarudrī states that since it is necessary for the phrase "because odor exists" to mean "because of the inference of odor," in that case...
The sense is that if the reason (*hetu*) is not adduced, the root [of the argument] would suffer from the fallacy of deficiency (*nyūnatā*). Regarding the term "useless" (*vyartha*):

the meaning is that if the stone were indeed earth (*pṛthivī*), the definition would be under-extended (*avyāpti*) to it; whereas if it were not earth, then because the absence of odor (*gandha*) in it serves to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*), the definition is favorable.

The meaning is that the actual state of things is not disregarded; for since it is an established tenet (*apasiddhānta*) that stone is not a substance other than earth, it is appropriate to avoid the charge of under-extension (*avyāpti*) by treating it as the definiendum (*lakṣya*).
Regarding the phrase "in the production of stone": and there is no destruction of odor even in the case of odor produced by heating (*pākaja-gandha*).

Otherwise, since the odor would be destroyed, it would follow that the odor would be produced by the cooking process even before [the destruction]; thus, it must be explained how the production of odor in an odorless atom is possible. [This is] because, with respect to odor, odor itself acts as a counteragent; therefore, it is precisely due to the absence of the non-existence of the contact with that counteragent [that the production occurs].

Because it is impossible for odor to arise in a sentient being [or in non-earth substances]. Nor should it be argued that, even so, since cooking produces odors born of cooking (*pākaja-gandha*) in water and other substances, it is necessary to establish earth-ness (*pṛthivītva*) as the cause of odor in order to exclude those cases;
for what constitutes "cooking" is precisely contact with fire of a different kind.
The sense is that, because one does not admit a difference in kind (*vaijātya*) in the case of contact with water and so forth. Regarding the word "substance" (*dravya*):

[an objection]—one might argue that what is intended here is being produced by destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) by virtue of being a destruction; thus, there would be no deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in this case, since for perception, the object is a cause generally by way of being an object (*viṣayatva*), and specifically...
Since it is sufficient [to explain the phenomenon] simply by way of that individuality as a cause, there is no evidence for an intermediate causal relationship; therefore, he says: "Alternatively...
Regarding "the array of bodies" (*kāyavyūha*): it refers to the [multiplication of bodies] by Saubhari and others for the purpose of quickly exhausting their *prārabdha* karma.
The simultaneous assumption of multiple bodies is heard of in the Purāṇas; in such a collection of bodies,
even the destruction of beginningless latent impressions (vāsanā) produced by false knowledge must be accepted as a cause for those who lack the knowledge of reality (tattvajñāna).
The meaning is that since the simultaneous assumption of multiple bodies is never experienced anywhere,

if one were to state [the definition] as "that which is produced by destruction," there would be a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of a collection of bodies that is not derived from the material cause (*upādāna*) of latent impressions (*vāsanā*). This refers to the view of the Neo-logicians (*Navīna*).

In the view of the moderns (*navīna*), since the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) of a staff are not admitted to be of the nature of the staff itself, there is no possibility of the aforementioned deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of a jar produced by a staff and so forth. Therefore, this was stated to indicate that the aforementioned purpose [of the definition] holds true according to that school's view. In the view of the ancients (*prācīna*), however, there is a deviation even in the case of a jar; hence, it was not included [in the definition].

Thus he says: "By the staff," etc. "Produced by the absolute absence of a substance that acts as an obstacle" means, for instance, fire produced by the absence of a jewel (maṇi). Regarding the phrase "in the opinion of the ancients": according to the view of the moderns, however, since the absolute absence of the obstacle itself is the cause of the effect, there is no such deviation (vyabhicāra).

It is called "bhāva" (existence) because it comes into being. Regarding the phrase "the body of a hell-being": one should not argue that there is no deviation [in the logical reason] because the performance of prohibited acts alone—by way of demerit—is the cause for both hell and the body conducive to it. This is because [the relationship is defined as] "having an activity conducive to itself" (*svānukūlakṛtimattva*). (Rāmarudrī)
The meaning is that even a prohibited action can function as a cause. Regarding the term "dadhnī" (in curd):

it means "sthūladadhnī" (in thick curd). Furthermore, the phrase "dugdhāvayava" (milk-constituent) also means "sthūladugdhāvayava" (thick milk-constituent). Even according to the established conclusion (siddhānta), [this applies to] the dyad of curd.

This is because [the opponent] accepts that [curd] is produced by the parts of the milk-dyad (dugdha-dvyaṇuka). Regarding the phrase "there is deviation" (vyabhicāra): the point is that although the curd-triad (dadhi-tryaṇuka) is produced from the destruction of the milk-triad (dugdha-tryaṇuka), it lacks the status of being produced from the material cause—the milk-dyad—which is itself a part of the milk-triad.
The phrase "distinct from dyads" (dvyaṇukātirikta) refers to this usage of the term "material cause" (upādāna).

This was stated with the intention of referring directly to the parts; however, if the phrase "that which is produced from that material cause" (tadupādānopādeya) means "produced by the atoms that constitute it," then there is no contradiction even in the case of thick curd, for although it is produced from the destruction of thick milk, it is nonetheless produced by the very atoms that constitute it.

In that regard, because [the property] exists, the status of being the originator of an atom can only be defined as possessing existence that necessitates its own existence; otherwise, since there would be no distinction in the consequence that ash—
being derived from the parts that originate a gross stone— would also possess the nature of a stone, [the definition would have to] extend all the way down to curd.
One must consider that there is simply an absence of purpose. Regarding the word "tasya" (of that): it means "the restriction of that.

In that context, regarding the curd dyad (*dadhi-dvyaṇuka*): [the phrase] "due to the lack of evidence" refers to the postulation that the atoms which constitute the milk move elsewhere, while different atoms which constitute the curd come here.

The sense is that [the production] is untenable due to the absence of its causal agent (*prayojaka*). "Otherwise" means: if the curd-dyad (*dadhi-dvyaṇuka*) were produced from milk-atoms (*dugdha-paramāṇu*), as stated in the *Rāmarudrī*. Now, one might object: there is indeed no evidence against a genus pervaded by what is pervaded by substancehood (*dravyatva*) residing in atoms.
To address this, he says: "by being curd" (*dadhitvena*), and so forth. Regarding the phrase "is a genus" (*jātīti*):

here too, both the state of being a genus (*vṛttitva*) and the state of possessing a genus (*jātimattva*) must be intended by way of inherence (*samavāya*) alone. Otherwise, if one were to take water-ness (*jalatva*) and earth-ness (*pṛthivītva*) [as examples], the fault of over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in water would remain as it was. And thus...

It should be understood that the exclusion of the term "jāti" (universal) is intended precisely to include properties such as "being both water and earth" (*jalapṛthivyubhayatva*). Regarding the word "apekṣā" (requisite cognition):

the duality residing in color is not of the nature of a number, because qualities are not admitted to reside in qualities; rather, it must be included as consisting in being the object of a requisite cognition whose objects are two colors.

The author of the Rāmarudrī, considering that [the definition] to be cumbersome because it involves [the destruction of form], formulated a definition involving the destruction of color (rūpa). The point is that since "destruction-ness" (nāśatva) is simply an indivisible (akhaṇḍa) upādhi, there is no cumbersomeness.
In the phrase "by way of involving duality, etc.," the word "etc. is included incidentally, as the remainder of the passage applies equally to both cases.

It should be understood that this is because of their equality. (35) Regarding the phrase "jātīti" (as regards the genus): here too, what was stated previously should be kept in mind. One might raise the objection: "Since 'earthness' (pṛthivītva) is also possible as a definition of earth, why was it not mentioned? He dispels this doubt with the words "atra ca" (and here). [The phrase] "in the opinion of the Teacher" (ācāryamata) [is used].

The cognition of positive concomitance (*anvayavyāpti*), characterized by pervasion and co-occurrence (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), is indeed the cause in every instance of inference. It may be objected that this being so, how can there be an inference in cases such as "Earth is distinct from others because it possesses odor," since the cognition of positive concomitance is impossible there?
This must be stated:
for in that case, it is accepted that the apprehension of positive concomitance (*anvayavyāpti*) occurs precisely through the apprehension of negative concomitance (*vyatirekasahacāra*).
Thus, *kevalānvayitva* (the state of being purely positive) consists simply in having a pervasion apprehended solely through positive concomitance. (Rāmarudrī on the reason).
The definition of a purely negative (kevalavyatirekin) inference is that its pervasion (vyāpti) is grasped solely through negative concomitance (vyatireka-sahacāra).
The view of the Teacher (Ācārya) is that an affirmative-negative (anvaya-vyatirekin) inference is one whose pervasion is grasped through the concomitance of both [positive and negative instances];
this is specifically the position of Maṇikāra, who maintains that the cognition of pervasion in both ways is the cause of inferential knowledge (anumiti).

It should be understood that "possessing a pervasion based on mere positive concomitance" and so forth refers to the state of being purely positively concomitant (*kevalānvayitva*) and the like. Regarding the phrase "of the delimitant of the subject" (*pakṣatāvacchedaka*):
at the very time of grasping the pervasion, [there is the grasping] of the subject-delimitant and the probandum, which are to be apprehended by the inference.
The meaning is that because the coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) has already been apprehended, there would be the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*).

"Because of non-contradiction" means that even a cognition with the same form but having a wider scope acts as an obstacle to inference, since it establishes exactly that which is already established. Although...

Furthermore, since the ancient masters accept that the understanding derived from the statement of the application (*upanaya*)— namely, "this [subject] is thus"— is precisely the cognition that "the subject possesses the reason," there is an impossibility of verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*) from the application statement when the property delimiting the subjecthood (*pakṣatāvacchedaka*) and the reason are identical; nevertheless, this applies only to inference for the sake of others (*parārthānumiti*).

In the view of the Neo-logicians (*navīna*), since the requirement for the application of formal reasoning (*nyāyaprayoga*) exists only in relation to inference for one's own sake (*svārthānumiti*), the purpose of the definition is fulfilled by that alone; thus, there is no deficiency even if verbal comprehension does not arise from the statement of the application (*upanayavākya*).

The sense is that since it is accepted that the cognition of the reason as being pervaded by the probandum (*sādhyavyāpyahetumad-bodha*) alone is produced by the application (*upanaya*), such [cognition] is possible because it involves a greater degree of comprehension regarding the element to be enjoined (*vidheya*). The phrase "all the more" (*sutarām*) is illustrative; it should be understood that the possibility of inference even with respect to the delimiting factor (*avacchedakāvacchedena*) is also to be recognized.
This is because the establishment of the mere fact of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) does not constitute an obstacle in that regard; such is the direction of the argument.
