The objection that the production of a perceptible aggregate of atoms from an imperceptible aggregate of atoms—as stated in the root text—is untenable because atoms are eternal—is refuted by the phrase "momentary destruction" (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*).
For their formal argument is as follows: whatever is existent is momentary, like a series of lamp-flames.

[The opponent's] position: "Because that which is invisible cannot have that which is visible as its material cause (*upādāna*). Regarding this, although the term *upādāna* cannot mean "cause" in general—since even in our own system, the invisible unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) is the cause of visible things such as jars—it likewise cannot mean "inherent cause" (*samavāyikāraṇa*).

Furthermore, since even they do not accept that an invisible atom (*adṛśya-paramāṇu*) is the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) of a visible atom (*dṛśya-paramāṇu*), if one were to accept that an atom exists in another atom by way of inherence (*samavāya*), it would follow that the atom itself possesses parts; consequently, the refutation of the composite whole (*avayavin*) would be untenable. Nor [does the word "atom"] have the sense of *prakṛti* (primordial matter).

For the state of being a material cause (*prakṛtitva*) consists in being the counter-positive of the destruction of that which produces itself, as seen in the case of curd with respect to milk and so forth. And this [state] is not possible in the case of atoms according to their view, because for those who maintain the doctrine of momentary flux (*kṣaṇabhaṅgavāda*),
[the atom] arises from each preceding individual instance.
Since the production of each subsequent individual [moment] is admitted, and since they do not accept an interval of even a single moment of destruction between them, this is highly inconsistent;
nevertheless, there is no logical inconsistency because the text is completed by the addition of "in your view" (*tvanmate*) and so forth. This is according to their own system.

It should be noted that since only the preceding manifestation (*pūrvavyakti*) is accepted as the cause of the subsequent manifestation, and the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) and so forth are not admitted as causes, there is no deficiency in taking the term "material cause" (*upādāna*) to mean "cause" in general. [The phrase] "due to independence from a cause" means that, according to your view, the state of being beyond the senses (*atīndriyatva*) [is established].
Since perceptibility is inherent, if that which is beyond the senses were to produce a sensory object,

it would follow that the eye and other organs would occasionally become visible; however, in my view, even though the triad (tryaṇuka) is perceptible by virtue of its instrumental capacity, [the sense organs do not share this property].

The point is that because of the absence of that [grossness], it is possible for the dyad (*dvyaṇuka*) to be beyond the senses; thus, there is no contradiction even if something imperceptible serves as the cause of something perceptible. Regarding the phrase "distinctive conjunction" (*vilakṣaṇasaṃyoga*), it means a conjunction of heterogeneous kinds (*vijātīyasaṃyoga*). And that heterogeneity—

The point is that one must simply accept the exclusion of contact with eye-demons (*cakṣuḥ-piśāca*) and the like; therefore, there is no contingency of those [atoms] becoming perceptible through mutual conjunction. By the use of the particle *eva*, it is indicated that "largeness" (*mahattva*) as something distinct from those [contacts] is not admitted.

It should be understood that since the mere composite whole (*avayavin*) is not admitted, and since even non-perceptible entities such as space (*ākāśa*) and time (*kāla*) are not admitted, it is impossible for [the definition of] "largeness" (*mahattva*) to apply to them. [The phrase] "because of the acceptance of arising and destruction" means that there is no consequence of the perception of arising and destruction occurring at every moment in objects such as a jar.
This must be stated: because, like a continuous stream of lamps for the purpose of illuminating a jar, perception of it is impossible due to its being uninterrupted;

for while perception is impossible when a perceptual aggregate lacks a preceding aggregate of the same kind and thus undergoes destruction, perception is possible when there is no subsequent such aggregate and thus production occurs.

The term "bhāvaḥ" (the state of being). "From the established doctrine" (siddhāntāt) means: according to the established doctrine that from two aggregates in the form of potsherds, a single aggregate in the form of a jar arises. "Dik" (direction/position): even though, according to the view of the author of the *Dīghiti*, the series of parts comes to rest in the triad (*tryaṇuka*) itself, and thus the aggregate of triads could be perceived—just like a mass of hair—nevertheless...

It has been indicated that the existence of a distinct whole (*avayavin*) is established precisely because it would be cumbersome (*gaurava*) to postulate that various triads (*tryaṇuka*) are the objects of such a cognition. Regarding the phrase "the consequence of [excessive] magnitude" (*mahattvāpatti*):
[this refers to the fact that] in relation to a diminished magnitude, [the cause is] by way of the relation of inhering in that which inheres in its own substratum (*svāśrayasamavetasamavetatva*).

Because number is a cause, [the suffix] *bhaviḥ* occurs here. "Of that which has become the cause" means: of that which brings about the increase or decrease of magnitude (*parimāṇa*). "Due to equality" (*sāmyāt*):
here, equality consists precisely in being the counter-positive of absences residing in both constituent parts; it is not...

It should be noted that if the series of parts were not to terminate, the very number residing therein would be unestablished, because there would be no uniformity of kind [in the series]. Regarding the phrase "due to a particular conjunction": just as it is established by experience that a fistful of cotton exhibits a gradation of magnitude due to a particular mode of accumulation (*pracaya*), so too...

The meaning is that the excellence of Mount Meru’s dimension is due to extremely loose conjunctions among its parts, whereas the inferiority of the mustard seed’s dimension is due to slightly loose conjunctions among its parts.
Regarding the phrase "by being regulated by a specific number": although [the number] of the parts...

Even when there is equality in number, a gradation in magnitude is experienced due to a difference in accumulation; nevertheless, the intended meaning here is that even with a much firmer conjunction, a reduction in magnitude is possible in the parts of a mustard seed. In reality, this applies to the parts of Mount Meru as well.
If one accepts a superior degree of accumulation in relation to the parts of a mustard seed, then it follows that Mount Meru must be softer than a mustard seed; this is the view of Rāmarudra.

It should be understood that [the objection] is sublated. Now, one might object: "Since even the proponents of our own school (siddhāntins) accept the production of destruction—which is an effect not inhering [in its cause]—this consequence is irrelevant. To this, he says: "an effect not inhering [in its cause]. [This refers to] the phrase "possessing multiple substances" in the root text.

The meaning is that [the property] consists in possessing multiple substances through the relation of inhering in that which inheres in itself (*svasamavetasamavetatva*). It does not mean that suchness [is established] through the relation of inherence (*samavetatva*);
for if it were so, the doubt regarding the lack of probative force (*aprayojakatva*) in the inference proving atoms would not be removed. (Rāmarudrī)

The object of meditation (*dhyeya*) is as follows: "by way of tradition" means that in cognitions such as "the jar is a substance," the property of being a jar (*ghaṭatva*) appears through the relation of inherence-in-its-own-substratum (*svāśrayasamavāyatva*). By the phrase "so they say," it is indicated that this fault does not apply if one accepts that "jar-ness" resides in a mere aggregate of triads (*tryaṇuka-puñja*) characterized by a specific kind of conjunction.
Thus, the lack of internal satisfaction [in that position] has been indicated by the phrase "due to the absence of proof," beginning with "in such a substance.

For although the dyad (*dvyaṇuka*) may be established through the otherwise inexplicable nature of the triad (*tryaṇuka*), which is established by perception, [there remains the problem of] a substance composed of three atoms (*paramāṇu*), and so forth.
The sense is that [the proof] is impossible. Regarding the term "due to parsimony" (*lāghavāt*):
it should not be argued that, in this case, its designation by the term "triad" (*tryaṇuka*) would be untenable;
for such usage occurs only among those whose mental impressions (*vāsanā*) regarding imperceptible dyads (*dvyaṇuka*) have been infused.

Since the term *trasareṇu* alone is employed in the Smṛti passage— "The subtle particle of dust that is seen in a sunbeam passing through a lattice is known as the first among measurements, called a *trasareṇu*"— that word, like words such as *maṇḍapa*, is purely conventional (*rūḍha*). Or else:

The sense is that the derivation of *reṇu* as "that which is devoid of dust" (*rajas*)— meaning one accompanied by three [atoms]— should be accepted there as an archaic usage (*ārṣa*) involving the elision of the *hita* suffix; for even compared to this,
there is greater parsimony (*lāghava*) in maintaining the eternity of the *tryaṇuka* (triad) alone, since the postulation of atoms (*paramāṇu*) and so forth involves complexity (*gaurava*).

The object of meditation (*dhyeya*) consists in being directed toward the cause (*hetuparatva*) and being directed toward the effect (*kāryaparatva*). Although the atom (*paramāṇu*) is indeed an object, it does not possess the status of being "such" (i.e., directed toward cause and effect) because the term "object" (*viṣaya*) in that context signifies an object that is produced (*janya*). Therefore, even further on in the verse, it says: "But the object is the dyad (*dvyaṇuka*) and so forth..."
The intention is that he will say, "the end of the cosmic egg" (*brahmāṇḍānta*); [this refers to] "born from a womb" (*yonija*) by way of the birth canal.

In the sense of "having emerged," there might be the objection that even a sweat-born being could possibly emerge through the vaginal door, leading to over-extension (*ativyāpti*); to avoid this doubt, he explains [the term] as "semen" (*śukra*). Regarding the phrase "of cattle, wild animals, and so forth": although the word *paśu* (cattle) [is used here].

Since the word "deer" (*mṛga*) already implies that which possesses hair, a tail, and so forth, the separate mention of the word "deer" in the collection of animals is redundant; nevertheless, it is either according to the maxim of "cattle and oxen" (*gobalīvardanyāya*),
or with the intention of including a specific type of deer that might lack a tail.

That is to be understood as its material cause (*upādāna*). By the phrase "birds and so forth," the inclusion of nests and the like is intended. Regarding the phrase "gadflies and so forth": one might raise the objection that even the bodies of worms and the like are produced from the union of semen and blood, since all bodies whatsoever are of such a nature; in response to this doubt, he says: "And of those bodies... [referring to the specific case].

"Of them" means of the bodies of gods and so forth, but not of the bodies of worms and so forth; this should be understood because the proof to be stated later does not establish the non-uterine birth (*ayonija*) of the latter. "Without a womb" [is the meaning].

The meaning is that it does not exist apart from semen and blood. Regarding the phrase "merely as a cause": [an objection is raised]—if this were so, since it is impossible for any effect whatsoever to exist without a cause, the statement that the body alone cannot arise without a cause would be untenable.

Anticipating this objection, he says: "the word 'body' (*śarīra-padam*). Here, the word "human" (*manuṣya*) is intended to include animals and so forth as well. Now, one might object: in order to establish that the human and other bodies possess the nature of earth, the reason (*hetu*) "because they possess smell and so forth" (*gandhādimattvāt*) was presented in the root text; in that reason, the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) is redundant.
Because pure odor alone is never non-deviant from being earth; nor should it be said that the word "etc.
(ādi) is intended to indicate other reasons, since that is impossible, as no other quality is ever non-deviant from being earth. Therefore:
He says: "by the words 'smell and so forth' (*gandhādi*)," etc.

Thus, the intention is that the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) is used precisely to indicate other causes such as blue color and the like. [In the commentary] *Rāmarudrī*, he says "sweat" because, since the body is not liquid, its oozing is impossible. Now, regarding "maturation" (*pāka*):

The conjunction with the fire that effects the transformation of form establishes only the nature of earth (*pṛthivītva*), and not the nature of fire (*tejastva*), because cooking is not admitted to occur in anything other than earth;
therefore, he says: "heat" (*auṣṇya*). This means the sensation of heat (*uṣṇasparśa*). "Arrangement" (*vyūha*) means action (*kriyā*).

Although possessing action (*kriyāvatva*) is not a prover of "air-ness" (*vāyutva*), because it is common to all five substances (*pañcadhātu*), nevertheless, since air alone possesses motion at all times, the term "action" here signifies "always possessing action"; thus, there is no inconsistency in proving air-ness by means of that. Nor...

In the state of deep sleep, there is no inconsistency in establishing the nature of air (vāyutva) by means of the body’s possession of motion, since it possesses such motion even then. Nor should it be argued that there is a lack of essential proof (svarūpāsiddhi) because the body lacks motion during the state of deep sleep; for even at that time—
The sense is that there is the existence of activity induced by breath and so forth. Regarding the phrase "of the four":

although the body arises from earth-atoms conjoined with water-atoms and so forth—just as a jar [arises from its constituent parts]—the three elements ending with air possess causality therein in the absence of connection with water.

Since no composite whole (*avayavin*) is produced due to the absence of conjunction, and since water and other elements cannot function as causes because they would never come into contact with heat, how can conjunction with space (*ākāśa-saṃyoga*) be a cause, given that it does not serve to differentiate [the location]? Nevertheless, because frogs and the like do not emerge from dense stones and such, space functions as the "opportunity" (*avakāśa*) for their birth.
It should be understood that this refers to being the cause of the body. "Viveka" means distinction.
"And not...
[refers to] Rāmarudrī.

The phrase "due to the absence of a decisive criterion" (*vinigamanāviraheṇa*) is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence]. "Being an action of that" (*tatkriyātva*) means being an action inherent in a body (*śarīrasamavetakriyātva*). Regarding "by way of overlap" (*saṅkareṇa*): earth-ness (*pṛthivītva*) is absent from the body-ness found in water-bodies and so forth, while body-ness is absent from the earth-ness found in jars and so forth.
The meaning is: "by the presence [of both] in the human and other bodies. "Accretion" (*upacaya*) means increase.

Regarding the word "therein" (*tatra*): the meaning is that such a wind possesses the nature of *prāṇa*. Because of its being a means of knowledge (*mānatvāt*), the attainment of a superior state through a specific quality makes it necessary for the tree to have a living body (*jīva-śarīratva*).

The sense is that it is possible for the very soul inhabiting that body to attain the highest state (utkramagati), and because there is a rule that the living self (*jīvātman*), which is the locus of experience, possesses vital breath (*prāṇavat*). Regarding the phrase "in a dead body":
one might ask, "Since movement existed previously even in a dead body, how can there be a lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*)? For when [movement exists], for whom... [the definition would apply].

It must be stated that its being a body consists in its possessing activity at that time; thus, the definition is one delimited by time. This is because the intention is that there would be a lack of pervasion (avyāpti) in cases where, immediately after death, another body has been produced—as in the case of Rāmarudrī. And although [the term] "hand-ness" lacks the status of a universal (jāti),...
Although over-extension (*ativyāpti*) would indeed follow by taking *pṛthivītva* (earthness) and so forth [as the probandum], nevertheless,

since it will be stated that this definition is over-extended to jars and the like when *pṛthivītva* and so forth are taken [as the probandum], it is improper to demonstrate its exclusion [from those] while taking them; therefore, [the author proceeds] to prove that *hastatva* (handness) is a genus (*jāti*).
[This is] the effort [involved]. Now, if "volitional movement" (*ceṣṭātva*), which enters into the definition of the body, is a specific universal (*jāti*) residing in the actions of the body,
then even in cases where an action arises in an insentient object such as a jar without being impelled by [physical] contact due to the power of a mantra,
there too— in accordance with the usage "the jar moves" (*ghaṭaś ceṣṭate*) through the power of the mantra— [it would follow that the jar possesses a body].

Since such a genus must be admitted, there would be an over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to jars and the like by taking "jar-ness" (*ghaṭatva*) as that genus. Furthermore, if "volitional effort" (*ceṣṭātva*) were defined as "the state of being a bodily action," then there would be the fallacy of self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*). Therefore, "volitional effort" is defined in another way—as follows: "volitional effort is... [The text continues: "...for the sake of exclusion; here, 'desirability' (*iṣṭatva*)."

Unwantedness (*aniṣṭatva*) consists in being the object of a desire delimited by itself, while [desirability] consists in being the object of an aversion delimited by itself. Therefore, even though actions such as the production of a jar may also be conducive to the attainment of what is desired or the avoidance of what is undesired for someone, there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) by taking "jar-ness" (*ghaṭatva*) and so forth as the basis. And "having that as its purpose" (*tadarthatva*) means having that as its motive (*tatprayojanakatva*).

This means "conformity with that. Nor should it be argued: "What kind of genus (*jāti*) must be taken in the case of the body so that the definition can be applied, since [geni such as] 'earthness' (*pṛthivītva*) and the like do not possess that property? For it is possible by taking [geni such as] "humanity" (*manuṣyatva*) and so forth. Nor is it the case that humanity is not a genus, [as one might think] because of [the presence of] "lionhood" (*siṃhatva*) and the like.
It should be stated that [the reason] is "due to confusion" (*sāṅkarya*). The sense is that in that case, [qualities such as] humanity (*manuṣyatva*) and so forth are not admitted [as universals].

Regarding the word "also" (*api*): it should be understood that while having only one individual instance (*ekavyaktikatva*) is the subverting argument (*bādhaka*) against *nṛsiṃhatva* being a universal (*jāti*), confusion is not. [End of] Rāmarudrī. Regarding "nine śarāvas": now, [one might object that] the non-manifestation of color and so forth...
That [definition] consists in not being a producer of that [perception].

And since this [condition] remains unimpaired even in the case of a particular instance of water that manifests odor but does not manifest color and so forth belonging to another, the intention is that by the word "only" (eva), there is no possibility of avoiding deviation in that case; thus, [the author] indicates its capacity to avoid deviation elsewhere.

He demonstrates this with the words "and in the mind" (*manasi ca*) and "the middle and the end" (*madhyāntam*). By the particle *eva* ("only"), the non-manifestation of anything other than odor and so forth is obtained; since that [non-manifestation] does not exist even in the olfactory organ (*ghrāṇendriya*), which is the manifestor of the nature of odor (*gandhatva*), the phrase "the middle and the end" is used along with the particle *eva* to prevent the fallacy of the unestablished nature of the reason (*svarūpāsiddhi*).

The meaning is that [the definition] is obtained as "not being the manifester of any one among smell, distinct form, and so forth"; therefore, there is no lack of essential nature (*svarūpāsiddhi*) even in the case of the olfactory faculty (*ghrāṇendriya*), which manifests the universal of smell (*gandhatva*). The meaning of [the term] "useless" is that it does not exclude deviation (*vyabhicāra*).

"Useful for the apprehension of pervasion" (vyāptigrahaupayikā) means "conducive to the apprehension of pervasion. For a qualifying attribute that excludes deviation (vyabhicāra) serves a purpose only insofar as it is conducive to the apprehension of pervasion; thus, if the middle term were not included [in the definition], it would apply to the reason itself.

The point is that since the existence of the subject (*pakṣasattva*) is not established—due to the impossibility of knowing the pervasion (*vyāpti*)—that [subject-existence] is also conducive to the apprehension of this very pervasion, and thus it is not useless.
Now, one might object: in this reason (*hetu*), the inclusion of "not being a manifester of sound" (*śabdāvyañjakatva*) is indeed purposeless, because of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*).
Even though [the substance] grasps taste, smell, and touch,

since it is possible for the reason to consist merely in being a manifester of smell while not manifesting taste, there is no purpose in including the non-manifestation of color and touch within the definition of the reason; therefore, [the author proceeds] by another method.
He begins to state the purport of that text with the words "this here" (*idam atreti*). Regarding the phrase "in the three reasons":

one might object that since the reasons consist of form, taste, touch, and sound, they are fourfold, and thus it is inconsistent to say "three"; therefore, he says "sound... and so on. [He refers to] "another alternative" (*kalpāntara*).

The meaning is: "a conceptualization not constituted by being owned by another. Thus, since even such water possesses the capacity to manifest its own touch, the sense is that there is no deviation (vyabhicāra) regarding the third reason.
By the word "api" (also/even), the previously mentioned parsimony (lāghava) is conjoined.

With the intention that even in the alternative beginning with "or else" (*yadvā*), the mention of all three—color, taste, and touch—within a single cause would be redundant, he says: "In that case also" (*tatrāpi*). Now, one might object: since the root text provides definitions only for the body and its objects, the implication is obtained that "sensory organ-ness" (*indriyatva*) is indeed a genus (*jāti*).
Anticipating the objection that this is not possible, he provides the following resolution: "The nature of being a sense-organ" (*indriyatva*).

Regarding "in relation to experience" (*upabhoge*): experience is the direct perception of pleasure and pain; its instrument is that which brings about such experience—this is the meaning. (Rāmarudrī: In that regard, because objects such as a jar are not causes [of experience]).

"The object of meditation" (dhyeyam) refers to "the earth in its form as an effect" (kāryarūpapṛthivyāḥ); the sense is that this is because of the explanation [in the commentary] that "it is in its form as an effect.
"As has been shown" (pradarśitaḥ): the sense is that in that context, the term "object" (viṣaya) means "an object that is produced" (janyaviṣaya). Although [the word] "that" (sā) [refers to...].

Even if there is no loss [to the definition] despite the fact that the state of being delimited by earth-ness (*pṛthivītva*) is not present in atoms, for although the largeness (*mahattva*) and so forth are impossible in an atom,
it is possible for it to be included within the threefold [classification] by way of being an object (*viṣayatayā*). Furthermore, regarding the word "and" (*ca*) in the phrase "that too" (*sā ca*),
[it serves to include] the threefold nature of water and the other elements which will be discussed later.

Since it is impossible for [the particle] to be a conjunctive particle (*samuccāyaka*) because another meaning is about to be stated, one must accept that it has the sense of the restrictive particle *eva*; and since water and the other elements are also threefold, it is impossible for it to exclude a threefold nature distinct from earth; therefore, [the word] "and" (*ca*)...

The sense is that it is necessary for the meaning to be precisely "of that which has the nature of an effect. [Regarding the phrase] "incidentally mentioned": the sense is that the state of being "entire" is already obtained by the word "all" (*sarvam*) itself.
Now, [one might object]: dependence on unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) is simply being produced by unseen merit, and that does not apply to effects such as jars and the like.

He raises the doubt that [the definition] is possible—[introducing it with] "here. Regarding the phrase "due to deviation" (*vyabhicārāt*): this is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*); even if [the relation] exists as such through temporal and spatial qualification (*viśeṣaṇatā*), one should understand that there is a deviation in that very same case. Regarding the word "should be understood": because even in the sky (*gagana*) there exists a conjunction with wind and so forth conjoined with the self (*ātman*).
The sense is that there is no deficiency even if one does not accept the conjunction of atoms with a distinct dimension (*vibhudravya-saṃyoga*).

Setting aside the phrase "produced by unseen merit" (*adṛṣṭajanya*), he begins to state the purpose of using the expression "dependent on unseen merit" (*adṛṣṭādhīna*) with the words "But this... (*idaṃ tu*). He says "it would be" (*syāt*); [this means] when all other causes are present, in the absence of that [unseen merit]. *Rāmarudrī*: [This refers to the case where] in the presence of all other causes, [the effect does not arise] due to its absence.
The meaning is that there is an absence of negative concomitance (*vyatireka-sahacāra*) in the form of the non-existence of the effect.

Its utility is the utility of the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*); the meaning is that in the absence of the unseen force that produces it, the production of its very causes would be impossible. But if this is so—
He dispels the doubt that the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) is irrelevant to every effect whatsoever by stating "in some cases" (*kvacit*).

The word "etcetera" (*ādi*) includes portents such as earthquakes and the like. "Otherwise" (*anyathā*) means if it were not a cause with respect to every effect. [The phrase] "the completeness of the causal complex in one place" (*sāmagrīsampattirekatra*)...

The relation delimited by the delimitors of all causes. Regarding the phrase "due to the impossibility": the sense is that the very nature of being a producer of an effect—which consists in the completion of the causal complex—is itself the nature of bringing about that causal complex. "Threefoldness" means possessing three differentiating properties.

The sense is that only mutually exclusive and pervading properties (*vyāpyadharma*) serve as differentiators. In the root text, the phrase "by another way" means "by means of having a body distinct from the object-ness (*viṣayatva*) and so forth. "Presentation" means "explanation. [This serves to bring about] clarity of the student's intellect.
The state of having as its object subordinate properties such as corporeality (*dehatva*) and so forth; that meaning is what constitutes its [the cognition's] determinant.

Although the contradiction regarding the classification is not thereby resolved, nevertheless, in the present context, "objectness" consists in being a means of experience distinct from the body and the sense organs.

It should be understood that there is no inconsistency regarding the division [of substances], because one accepts that [the property of being a cause] is delimited by the status of being a differentiator (*vibhājakatāvacchedakatva*). Thus ends the section on Earth (38). Now, an objection: even if "water-ness" (*jalatva*) is established as the delimitor of the generative capacity for viscidity (*sneha*), its status as a universal (*jāti*) is not thereby established.

In response to the objection that, since the property of being a cause (kāraṇatātva) in relation to sound and so forth is not invariably concomitant with being delimited by a universal (jātyavacchinnatva), it is impossible to prove that [the cause] is delimited by the universal "water-ness" (jalatvajāti) by means of that reason, he says: "because there is no subverting evidence" (bādhakābhāvāt). [The word] "jātitva" [refers to the nature of being a universal].

This is the remainder [of the sentence]. The meaning is that there is an absence of subverters (*bādhaka*) of a universal (*jāti*), such as the non-difference of individuals (*vyaktyabheda*). The word "due to parsimony" (*lāghavāt*) is to be supplied after the phrase "the state of being a universal" (*jātitvam*). By this, it is shown that the water-ness (*jalatva*) which serves as the delimiting factor of causality (*kāraṇatāvacchedaka*) is simply the possession of cold touch (*śītasparśavatva*), and not a universal.
The objection that it is cumbersome to postulate a distinct category (*padārthāntara*) has been refuted;

for, due to the complexity of positing multiple entities qualified by the genus "coldness" (*śītatva*) as the delimitors of causality (*kāraṇatāvacchedaka*), it is simpler (*lāghava*) to posit the mere genus "pure water-ness" (*śuddhajalatva*).

It should be understood that this is because it is appropriate for [the property] to be the delimiting condition of the causal status (*kāraṇatāvacchedakatva*). Regarding the phrase "due to the absence of defects":

[this refers to] the effect-status (*kāryatā*) consisting in the property of being water-ness, which is the non-delimiter of the counter-correlativity of an absence residing in a locus delimited by a specific time and qualified by the possession of oiliness (*snehavatva*).
The sense is that it is impossible for "oiliness" (*snehatva*) not to be over-extended [to other substances]. Regarding the phrase "here too":
the meaning is "even in the case of an atom that does not produce oiliness. "In the same way, here too it will be so":

the meaning is that there will be no contradiction with respect to that which possesses "water-ness" (*jalatva*) as the delimiting condition of causality (*kāraṇatāvacchedaka*). Now, [an objection]:...

"Being produced water" (*janyajalatva*) means "the nature of water qualified by being produced" (*janyatvaviśiṣṭajalatva*); and since a qualified entity (*viśiṣṭa*) is not a universal (*jāti*), he says: "only produced water" (*janyajalamātra*). "In the ultimate part of water" (*jalāntyāvayavini*) refers to a water-part that is incapable of generating another water-entity. "It would not exist" (*na syāt*) [refers] in such water.
The point is that if one accepts a genus (*jāti*) as the delimiting factor of productivity (*janakatāvacchedaka*), then that [water] would simply lack such capacity.

"Because it is not admitted" means that since the capacity to produce a large mass of water exists in mere water through its conjunction with other water. "From the establishment of the genus" [is said]; but [an objection may be raised]: nanu...
Since there is an absence of a decisive criterion (*vinigamanāviraha*) regarding water-ness (*jalatva*) as well, [the author] says:

"Because of the absence of an absence of a decisive criterion. For the status of being a delimiting factor of causality (*kāraṇatāvacchedakatva*) for that which is yet to be postulated is established by the means of knowledge that apprehends the subject (*dharmigrāhakapramāṇa*), whereas for that which is already established (*klṛpta*), it is not so; thus, this very point serves as the decisive criterion.

The meaning is "because of existence. "Without dispute" refers to the phrase beginning with "by means of positive and negative concomitance" (*anvaya-vyatirekābhyām*). "As distinct entities" is stated in accordance with the actual state of things (*vastugatimanurudhya*); for even though fire is the cause of smoke by virtue of being the fuel (*indhana*) for the fire, [the two remain distinct].

It should be noted that the establishment of "water-ness" (jalatva) is possible precisely by its inclusion within the scope of the delimiting condition of the causal capacity (*kāraṇatāvacchedaka*). The phrase "they say" (*āhuḥ*) indicates a lack of final satisfaction; the reason for this is that if the conjunction of water with the form of an atom (*paramāṇu-rūpa-jala-saṃyoga*) were the cause of smoke, [it would lead to an over-extension].

This is because, by the aforementioned reasoning, the property of being water (*jalatva*) is not established in an atom due to the absence of proof. As for the phrase "others, however" (*pare tu*) and so forth, that is indeed his own view; for he himself previously stated that there is no deficiency even if "being produced" (*janyatva*) is not included, since it is possible for the property of oiliness (*snehatva*) alone to serve as the delimiting factor of being produced (*janyatāvacchedaka*).

It must be considered that [the definition] is included therein. Now, if the state of being neither pervaded by nor non-pervaded by substanceness (*dravyatva*) were simply the nature of being directly pervaded by substanceness, then there would be the fault of over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to color and so forth, since they possess such a nature; therefore, he says: "like color," and so on.
